## Five-hundred-and-thirty-second round: the killer sees the death -- a hold set when the result arrives, the clip played as the blow lands

On the screen of the player who landed the killing blow, the monster did not die: it vanished. Every
other player's client in the zone plays its die animation, from the zone's `OpMonsterDied` push
(`_on_monster_died`). Both are read from the code below, not watched or timed in a run.

**Why, read in the code.** The server tells the zone about a kill with `OpMonsterDied`, and it sends
that push to everyone *except* the attacker: `session/combat.go` `performAttack` builds its
broadcast list with `e.Session.ID() != sess.ID()`, and `session/gm.go`'s `/kill` does the same.
The killer learns of the death only from its own `OpAttackResult`. On the client:

- `_on_attack_result`'s deferred blow skipped the hit reaction when the blow killed, and animated
  nothing in its place. Its comment said the die animation "comes from the list sync" (round 208).
- The handler ends with a synchronous `NetClient.list_monsters()`, and that reply no longer names
  the monster.
- `_sync_monster_bodies` frees every body the list does not name, unless `_dying_until` holds it,
  and erases `_monster_assembled` with it. After that `_play_monster_action` has nothing to play.
- Only `_on_monster_died` set `_dying_until`, and that is the handler for the push the killer never
  gets.

So, going by the code, the body went on the first list reply after the result. That reply was
expected a frame or two later; no run has measured it (see "Not measured" below).

**The fix.**

- `MonsterBodies` (`client/scripts/world/monster_bodies.gd`) holds the rule. `should_free` is
  today's test, unchanged: free an id the list does not name unless a hold keeps it.
  `hold_for_kill` is new: it sets `dying_until[id]` to `now + lands_after + die_seconds`, keeping
  any later hold, and sets nothing when `die_seconds` is 0.
- `_on_attack_result`, on a kill, calls `hold_for_kill` **before** the deferred blow is scheduled
  and before its trailing list request. `lands_after` is the swing's own hit event, the value the
  handler already waits on (`EVENT_HIT`; its millisecond unit is inferred from the numbers,
  `docs/protocol/BSR_FORMAT.md` "Events and walk points"). `die_seconds` is the die clip's own
  length, from the new `_monster_action_seconds`. That does `_play_monster_action`'s lookup without
  playing, and returns 0 wherever `_play_once` would play nothing (a clip of one frame or fewer).
- The deferred blow now calls `_begin_monster_death` when it killed. That is `_on_monster_died`'s
  old body, factored out: clear the target if it is this monster, drop a walk toward it, play type
  4 (`die` in mangnyang's `default` group, BSR_FORMAT.md) held on its last frame, and set the hold
  again from the clip's real start, with a timer that asks for the list when it ends.
  `_on_monster_died` calls it and then asks for the list, as before.
- When `_begin_monster_death` plays nothing while a kill hold is set, it lifts the hold and asks for
  a list. Otherwise no timer would come, and the body would stay until some unrelated refresh.
- New log lines, so a run can be timed: `monster N killed by own blow t=T, clip starts in L`,
  `monster N dies, holding S t=...`, `monster N body removed t=R`. The existing `attack hit ...`
  line gains `t=`. `t` is `_idle_anim_time`, the clock the hold is kept on.

**What a player sees change.** The killer's monster plays its death where it fell, held on the last
frame until the clip ends, then goes. The killer's target window now closes when the death clip
starts. Before, nothing cleared the target on an own kill: `_clear_target` was reached only from
`_on_monster_died`.

**Measured (headless, render box).** `monster_bodies_test.gd` uses fixture numbers: a 0.651 s hit
event and a 1.4 s clip. They stand in for the real ones; the rule is what is under test. After
`hold_for_kill(d, 7, 10.0, 0.651, 1.4)`, a list that omits 7 does not free the body at 10.005 or at
11.9, and does free it at 12.052. The other cases:

- A live id is never freed.
- An id with no hold is freed.
- `die_seconds` 0 sets no hold.
- A later existing hold is kept.
- A clip-start hold written over the predicted one is honoured.

With `hold_for_kill` still the no-op it was at the refactor step (today's killer path, which sets
no hold), the suite reported 2 FAILURES, the NEGATIVE among them: the list 5 ms after the kill
freed the body. Implemented: ALL PASS. `remote_godot.sh tests`: 82 suites, 0 failing. `check`: 249
scripts and 5 scenes load.

**Not measured: the live run.** This round used the render box only through `remote_godot.sh`,
which runs the headless suites and renders nothing. The box does have a server at `qa_shot.sh`'s
default `SERVER_BIN`. `/opt/srrevamp-server/srrevamp-server` is an executable 64-bit ELF of
15,276,922 bytes, dated 2026-09-19 04:04 (`stat`, `file`), so the script's `-x` guard passes.
But that is a 2026-09-19 build, older than this tree: `git log --since` counts 129 commits under
`server/` newer than it. The check still to run should use a server built from this tree, passed
as `--server <host:port>`:
`SRREVAMP_QA_ATTACK_FAST=1 SRREVAMP_QA_ATTACK_NAME=Mangyang SRREVAMP_QA_ATTACK_GOTO=1 qa_shot.sh
--server <host:port> --attack --frames 900 --out /var/tmp/mob_killer_death`. For each `killed by
own blow t=T, clip starts in L` line, a `dies, holding S` line should follow, and the matching
`body removed t=R` should have R >= T + L + S - 1/60. Before this fix, R - T was expected to be one
or two frames. Neither number has been measured. Delete the frames afterwards.

**Not covered headlessly, so do not tag before the live check.** `monster_bodies_test.gd` tests
`MonsterBodies` only. Nothing headless covers the World3D wiring: that `hold_for_kill` runs
before `_on_attack_result`'s trailing `list_monsters()`, that `_monster_action_seconds` matches
`_play_monster_action`, or `_begin_monster_death`'s branch for a clip that did not play. The live
check above is what would cover them. The round is worth a release, but its tag waits for that
check.

**Residual races, disclosed in the code at `hold_for_kill`:**

- A keep-up swing sends its `OpAttackResult` from the keep-up goroutine
  (`session/keepup.go` `autoAttack.loop`, which calls `performAttack`). `OpMonsterList` is answered
  on the session's reader. A list reply can therefore overtake a keep-up kill's result, and free
  the body before any hold exists. This is the **usual** kill path, not a special case. The
  `OpAttack` handler in `session/combat.go` swings once and then, under the comment "One click is
  the whole fight", calls `armKeepUp`. `Arm` starts the goroutine (`go a.loop`). So every kill
  past the first swing comes from that goroutine. The window itself is narrow. A list request has
  to be handled on the reader after the kill's `ApplyDamage` in `performAttack` (the hub deletes
  the id there, `internal/combat/combat.go` `Hub.ApplyDamage`) and before the goroutine's
  `sess.Send` of the result. The previous swing's own trailing request was answered a swing
  earlier. A request in the window has to come from somewhere else, for example another player's
  damage or died push, a death clip's end timer, or the refresh button.
- A GM `/kill` still vanishes on the GM's own screen. `session/gm.go` refreshes the GM's list, sends
  the GM no died push, and no attack result passes through `_on_attack_result`.

**Other residuals found in review, not changed here:**

- **A click can target a corpse.** The real click picker, `_try_attack_monster`, targets any body
  with a `monster_id` meta, dying or not. `_step_pending_attack` and the QA picker
  (`_qa_click_target_for`) skip `_dying_until` ids; `_try_attack_monster` does not. The killer's
  corpse now stays up for about `lands_after` plus the die clip, so a click on it opens the target
  window on a dead monster. The attack then goes nowhere. With a reach band, `_step_pending_attack`
  drops it at once. With no band, `_attack_monster` sends it and the server answers "target not
  found". Nothing closes the window afterwards. Other players' corpses already behaved this way;
  this round extends it to the killer's.
- **The two clocks can disagree.** The hold is kept on `_idle_anim_time`, which `_physics_process`
  advances (through `_tick_idle_animations`). The end-of-clip `SceneTreeTimer` counts process
  time. If physics falls behind (a low frame rate), the list that timer asks for can arrive while
  `_idle_anim_time` is still short of the hold. Then `should_free` keeps the body, and no further
  timer is set, so the corpse holds its last frame until some unrelated list refresh. The
  `_on_monster_died` path already had this, and the killer's path now shares it. Not measured.
- **A late blow from an earlier swing can replace the held die clip.** The earlier swing's deferred
  closures (its `TYPE_HIT`, or the counter-swing's `TYPE_ATTACK`) can land after the die clip has
  started. `_play_once` then replaces the die entry. The die entry has no resume, so the late clip
  holds its own last frame instead. This needs two swings whose hit events are further apart than
  the swing interval. A non-killer's late blow after `OpMonsterDied` has the same problem. Both
  predate this round. A killing result itself carries no counter-swing: `performAttack`'s
  counterattack is in the branch for a monster that did not die.

## Five-hundred-and-tenth round: NPCs face open space -- a disclosed stand-in

Reported right after round 506: the buildings turned correctly, but "the NPCs are still facing the
wrong cardinal direction". They are placed by a different path (`_try_spawn_region_npcs`), which
set a position and no rotation at all, so every NPC faced the way its model was authored -- the same
way for all of them.

**The game's facing is data this project does not have.** The server spawns every NPC facing the
direction stored in its nest row: `Nest_Hatch` (`0x005607b0`) reads the row's u16 at `+0x1c` --
`Tab_RefNest.wInitialDir` -- and converts it to radians as `wInitialDir / 65535.0 * 360.0 * pi/180`
(`fdiv [0xb45c28]` 65535.0, `fmul [0xb45c30]` 360.0, `fmul [0xb45e00]` pi/180, at `0x5609ce` and
`0x560a2a`); monsters instead roll a random facing (`rand / 32767 * 2pi`), except rarity 3.
`TAB_REFNEST` / `CRefNest` are the server binary's own names for the table. None of it ships in a
file: `npcpos.txt` has exactly five columns (id, region, x, y, z) on all 12,367 rows; Media, Data and
Map.pk2 hold no nest, hive, tactics or spawn table (searched by name); the server package on the RE
box carries binaries, the cert module, SMC, tools and web scripts but no database backup.

**The stand-in, chosen with the user and disclosed as own design:** `NpcFacing.open_direction` faces
an NPC toward the most open space around it, measured on the region's own navigation graph with the
walk a character makes (`NavGraph.step_tracked`), so walls, doorways and the object it stands on count
as they do for a player. 24 headings are walked outward (20-unit steps; a step that makes less than
half a step of progress has met a wall), at 80, then 160, then 320 units until the headings disagree;
each heading is scored over its +-30-degree sector and the NPC faces the MIDDLE of the longest run of
best-scoring headings (the first maximum would be the edge of the open side). An NPC open on every
side at 320 units keeps its old facing rather than getting an arbitrary one. The holder rotation puts
the body's front -- its own local -Z, the playtest-settled convention the player body uses -- along the
chosen direction: `atan2(-dir.x, -dir.z)`.

**Measured on the render box:** in Jangan all 18 placed NPCs (and 23 in the four neighbouring regions)
got a facing; none was open all round. The cost at region load is 404 ms for Jangan's 18 (708 ms at
10-unit steps). `npc_facing_test` pins a wall east (faces west, the middle of the open arc, not its
edge), a wall north, a corner (faces the open diagonal), all-open (no facing), a wall found only at a
longer range, and that the holder rotation points the body's front along the choice.

**Not the game's value, and said so in the code:** an NPC the game turns toward a wall, or along a
street, will not match. The real fix is importing `Tab_RefNest.wInitialDir` (docs/TODO.md) and
applying it with the formula above.

## Five-hundred-and-sixth round: every turned object faced the wrong way

Reported from a playtest: "almost every asset is in the wrong cardinal direction". It was true of
every placed object whose yaw is not 0 or 180 degrees -- in Jangan that is every shop (the stable,
armour, weapon and general stores and `cj_luxury` all sit at 90 or 270), every `c_sta_01` statue,
the portal and most trees -- and it had been true since placements were first rotated.

**The cause.** `World3D` set `node.rotation.y = yaw` and `NavGraph.place` built
`Basis(UP, yaw)`, feeding the game's raw angle straight to Godot. The field was right; the
direction of turn was not. The game turns objects the other way.

**Read from the binary, not inferred.** The client's own navmesh loader,
`MapLoader::FUN_0042b8b0` (`JMX_Library\navmesh\MapLoader.cpp`, "Load Fail(NavMesh Obj)"),
builds every navmesh object from its placement record: position from the record's words 1..3, and
the float at record `+0x12` -- the yaw, the same offset the `.o2`/`.nvm` readers use -- handed to
`FUN_0043cda0`. That function zeroes a 4x4 float matrix and writes

	m[0] = m[10] = cos(yaw)    m[2] = sin(yaw)    m[8] = -sin(yaw)    m[5] = m[15] = 1

(`0x43cded..0x43cdfb`). Which call is which was settled from the code, not the names: `0xb44a10`'s
x87 fallback executes `fcos` (`0xb44a7d`), `0xb44b40`'s executes `fsin` (`0xb44bad`). The matrix is
a Direct3D row-vector one -- the render-side callers write the object's position into `m[12..14]`
(`CImitationObj::vslot_027` at `0x9c3d90`, `FUN_009cf600` at `+0x30/+0x34/+0x38`), so a vertex is
placed as `v * M + position`, sending local +X to `(cos, 0, sin)` and local +Z to `(-sin, 0, cos)`.
Godot's `Basis(UP, a)` sends +X to `(cos a, 0, -sin a)`, so the game's turn is `a = -yaw`, in the
raw coordinates both the rendered objects and the navigation graph are placed in (the terrain
group's global `z -> -z` mirror applies after, to everything alike).

**Measured against the game's own data as well**, with a new headless probe,
`client/tools/check_object_yaw.gd`, which places every navmesh object's own navigation mesh under
eight candidate conventions (plus/minus yaw, each with 0/90/180/270 offsets) and scores each against
the region's `.nvm`:

- **Linked edges** (the only object-to-object edge links; Jangan's bridge spans, 6 links): mean
  midpoint gap **1.48** under the negated yaw, **58.4** under the positive one, 186-322 under the
  others.
- **Footprint precision** (a placed triangle's centroid lands in a cell that lists the object),
  over objects not at 0/180 in 57 regions across the map: **99.3%** negated, 97.2% positive,
  94-96% for the 90-degree offsets.
- **Where the doors face.** Jangan's west-side shops open east onto the square under the negated
  yaw: the weapon shop (at x 142) has its doorway edges (flag 0) at x 312, the armour shop (x 191)
  at x 318, the stable (x 247) at x 309 and 363. Under the positive yaw each would open west into
  the town wall.

**What was wrong with the earlier confirmation.** `MAPO_FORMAT.md` recorded the yaw as confirmed by
a decompiled `(cos, 0, sin)` construction in `FUN_009f2c20`. That function is `SWorld::vslot_026`,
which builds a positioned source with two radii -- not an object placement -- so it confirmed the
field and never the direction. The other half was a picture: a straight city-wall run "reads as one
continuous wall", which it does under either turn. The one check that would have caught it, the
navmesh's own linked edges, sat in the parsed data unused.

**The fix.** `NavGraph.godot_yaw(engine_yaw) = -engine_yaw` holds the conversion, with the binary
citations, and both call sites use it -- the rendered object (`World3D`) and its navigation mesh
(`NavGraph.place`, which `walk_probe` also uses) -- so what a player collides with still matches what
they see. The reader and format docs (`mapo_reader.gd`, `mapo2_reader.gd`, server `mapo.go` /
`mapo2.go`, `MAPO_FORMAT.md`) carry the correction. `nav_graph_test` pins the game's matrix directly
(90 and 30 degrees) and its rotated-ramp case now expects the game's turn: the old case expected the
opposite one, because it pinned the project's convention rather than the game's.

**Checked unaffected:** the spawn at local (1002, 1020) still stands on `cj_jang_gate` and walks
north with no wall contact, identically under both conventions (the plaza is at 0/180). The server
only reports the angle (`cmd/whatishere`) and transforms nothing.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-seventh round: the message buffer, and a hunch that was right in the wrong place

Chasing the use-item payload a third time. `Item_HandleUseItem` never touches
`+0x1050`, the message -- it reads a word at `+0x103e` over and over, which
looked like a parsed field.

It is not. `MsgBuf_ReadUInt8` (`0x00404f80`) is **already named and annotated**
in this repo, and says what those offsets are: buffer `+0x1034`, read cursor
`+0x103c`, size `+0x103e`. The handler was checking the message **size**.

### The writer completes the map

`0x00404090` is called eight times by that one handler and also by
`Msg_SendTwoFieldReply`. It is the append:

	if (this[0x104c] < AX + this[0x103e]) throw     ; capacity
	memcpy(this[0x1034] + this[0x103e], src, AX)    ; append at the size
	this[0x103e] += AX
	*(ushort *)this[0x1054] = (*(ushort *)this[0x1054] & 0x8000) | (this[0x103e] - 6)

Filed as `MsgBuf_AppendBytes`. Two new fields fall out -- `+0x104c` capacity and
`+0x1054`, a **pointer to the on-wire header's Size word**.

### The 6, confirmed from the other side

`size - 6` is the payload length, so the header is **six bytes** and bit
**`0x8000`** of the Size word is reserved. Both were already recorded in
`opcodes/handshake.md`, read from the **checksum** side: *"(Size & 0x7fff) + 6
bytes ... including the real 6-byte header"*. Two independent routes to the same
frame.

**And this does not revive the hypothesis round 326 killed.** That one read a
byte at `+6` of `this->[0x30]` -- a different object entirely. The header is
real; it simply was not there. **A correct constant found in the wrong place is
still the wrong place**, and killing it was right even though the number turned
out to be the header size after all.

### What it buys

Round 324 left 93 real handlers whose remaining work is "the payload layout".
Every one reads its payload through `MsgBuf_Read*` against this buffer, so a
handler's layout is **the sequence of those calls** -- a greppable question now,
not a reading one. That is the tool the last three rounds were missing.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-sixth round: the handler ABI, and round 323 redone properly

Two things, and the first makes the second cheap.

### The handler ABI, read from the dispatcher

`server_dispatch.md` records how a handler is *found*. How it is *called* was
not written down, and every one of the 162 handlers needs it:

	50ef08  mov   eax,[esi+0x1050]    ; the received message
	50ef0e  movzx ecx,WORD PTR [eax]  ; its opcode -- the message's first word
	50ef27  push  esi                 ; THE ARGUMENT: the session object
	50ef4f  call  edx                 ; handler(this = pc + adjustor, esi)

So a handler takes **one stack argument, the session object**, and reaches the
message through `session+0x1050` -- not the message itself. That is why
`Item_HandleUseItem` opens with `mov esi,[ebp+0x8]` and then reads
`[esi+0x1054]`.

**A hypothesis this killed.** A `mov cl, BYTE PTR [eax+0x6]` inside the handler
looked like a payload read six bytes into the packet -- and six is exactly the
real Silkroad header (size, opcode, count, CRC), which is the kind of
coincidence that gets written up. Reading the two instructions above it shows
`eax` is `this->[0x30]`, another object entirely. Not a header.

### Round 323, redone soundly

The same disassembly showed the real shape of a refusal:

	push 0x185f          ; the ERROR CODE, pushed
	mov  ecx,0xb04c      ; the REPLY OPCODE, in ECX
	call 0x4e7250

Both immediates, neither the decompiler's argument. That makes a sound sweep
greppable, so all **256** call sites in `.text` were done properly:

| | |
|---|---:|
| with an ECX immediate | 251, of which **247 are `0xbXXX`** |
| pushing an error code | 72 sites, **59 distinct codes** |
| of those, named by the client | 38 (64 %) |
| **pushed but with no client `case` anywhere** | **15** |

	0x1403  0x1807  0x1811  0x181d  0x1c0d  0x1c0e  0x3c0f  0x3c2a
	0x3c32  0x3c33  0x480f  0x4828  0x4c33  0x6006  0x6008

Six lookalikes are handled after all (`0x6415`/`0x6416` in the main switch,
`0x8006`-`0x800a` elsewhere), which is why it is fifteen and not twenty-one.

**The membership changed, which is the whole point of redoing it.** `0x1806`
drops out and `0x1403`, `0x480f`, `0x4828` appear -- so round 323's list was not
merely ill-derived, it was wrong, and three real codes were missing from it.

**And one is corroborated from elsewhere.** `0x4828` is what `jobs.md` records
the job-join handler returning for a kind outside {1,2,3}, read in round 273
from another function on another day. A refusal a player can trigger, with no
message behind it.

The use-item payload is still unread -- two rounds now -- but the ABI above is
what the next attempt needs, and it is written down.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-fifth round: round 323 was wrong, and the function it rested on is now named

Round 324's next probe was "take one named handler and recover its payload", so
this round opened `Item_HandleUseItem` (real opcode `0x04c`). The payload is not
what it found.

Four instructions into the handler:

	5109de  mov ecx,0xb04c        <- the REPLY OPCODE
	5109e5  call 0x4e7250

**`0xb04c` is a reply opcode, not an error code** -- and round 323 had just
built a finding on the premise that `FUN_004e7250` is "the refusal sender" whose
argument is a refusal code. Reading it settles the matter:

	FUN_004e7250(opcode):            ; opcode in ECX
	    msg = this->slot_0x278(opcode)
	    append two words from the caller's frame
	    this->slot_0x27c(msg)

It is a **generic two-field reply helper**. The error code is one of the two
appended words and arrives in a *different* register. At `0x51170f` the
composite-item handler sets `ebp = 0x18c6` (PREMIUM_USE_OVER) and
`ecx = 0xb15f` (the reply opcode) before calling it -- both, in different
registers.

### Why round 323's list is withdrawn

Its thirteen codes came from grepping the decompiled C for
`FUN_004e7250(0x...)`. At the very call site that produced `0x1806` the
disassembly reads `mov ecx,0xb034` -- Ghidra had named a **payload** value as
the argument. Across sites it resolves sometimes to the opcode and sometimes to
the payload, so the grep collected a mixture.

**The evidence was in round 323's own output and I explained it away.** The list
included `0x3`, `0x5` and `0xb`, which I dismissed as "not error codes, my grep
caught other arguments" -- when the right reading was that the extraction could
not tell arguments apart at all, and therefore could not be trusted for the rest
either.

What survives is weaker and honest: those values are not valid reply opcodes
(replies are `0xbXXX`) and they sit among named errors, so they are *plausibly*
error codes. Whether the server emits them is **not established**.

### What the round leaves behind

`FUN_004e7250` filed as `Msg_SendTwoFieldReply`, with a warning at the row that
Ghidra's argument for it is unreliable -- so the next person does not repeat the
sweep. And the sound method, partly run: reading registers per call site over 38
resolvable sites gives 19 distinct ECX values of which **16 are `0xbXXX`**,
confirming ECX is the opcode. The three that are not -- `0x3156`, `0x34a8`,
`0x34aa` -- are a loose end worth its own look.

The use-item payload itself is still unread. Chasing a wrong premise cost the
probe, which is the honest accounting of this tick.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-fourth round: how far the protocol actually is from real

`SYSTEMS.md` has carried **"opcode coverage vs the real space is unmeasured"**
as the packet row's next probe for as long as the row has existed. Both halves
were already in the repo -- `message_handlers.tsv` (the client's registration
table) and `server_handlers.tsv` (the server's request indices) -- so this is a
join, not a dig.

| | |
|---|---:|
| real opcodes the client registers a handler for | **318** |
| real server request indices | **162** |
| opcodes srrevamp declares | **143** |
| **srrevamp opcodes that are real ones** | **0** |

**Zero is the right answer and not a failure.** `PROTOCOL_DECISION.md` reversed
the project's direction on 2026-08-22 to a full wire-level reimplementation and
says of the current numbers, in its own words, that they are *"placeholder
scaffolding, not the destination"*. What had never existed is a number for the
distance to that destination.

### The useful half: 93 of 162 real handlers are already named

**57 %** of the real server-side request surface has a named function in the
dump, and 115 of 162 exist there at all. For those the handler is identified, so
the work left per opcode is the **payload layout**, not finding the code. The
list is now in `PACKET_FORMAT.md` as a roadmap rather than a statistic.

Several land on systems srrevamp ships today: `GObjPC_HandleShopMsg_046`,
`GObjPC_HandleIncreaseStr`/`IncreaseInt` (`0x050`/`0x051`), four party handlers
-- and `Item_HandleUseItem` at real opcode **`0x04c`** replying **`0xb04c`**,
which is the same message this project relocated to `0x008a` three rounds ago
after it collided with party-create.

### Why nothing was changed

Adopting the number without the layout would be **worse than the placeholder**:
a real client would connect, recognise `0x04c` and then misread every byte after
it. `PROTOCOL_DECISION.md` requires the wire number *and* the payload layout
before an opcode moves, so this round measures and records and moves nothing.

The row's next probe is now specific: take one named handler and recover its
payload.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-third round: thirteen refusals the client cannot render

Round 322 ended noting three codes absent from `error_codes.md`. That page is
built from the CLIENT's switch, so an absence there might only mean "not a
user-facing refusal". Asking the **other** side settles it: which codes does the
server actually hand out?

`FUN_004e7250` is the refusal sender -- **256 call sites**. Of the literal codes
passed to it, **thirteen appear as a `case` nowhere in the decompiled client**:

	0x1806  0x1807  0x1811  0x181d
	0x1c0d  0x1c0e
	0x3c0f  0x3c2a  0x3c32  0x3c33
	0x4c33  0x6006  0x6008

**They are holes inside mapped families.** The client names `0x1810`
STRGERR_HIGHER_LEVEL_REQUIRED, `0x1812` STRGERR_LOCKED_BY_OTHER_ONE and `0x181e`
STRGERR_BUSY, while `0x1806`, `0x1807`, `0x1811` and `0x181d` sit among them
with nothing -- so the family is mapped and these specific members are not. A
player triggering one gets the dispatcher's default, not a reason.

`0x8006`-`0x800a` looked identical and are not: they have cases in a different
client file. Checking that is the difference between thirteen and seventeen.

### The part I got wrong first, and what it cost

Counting `case` labels in the switch gives **643** against the page's **605**,
which reads as 38 missing rows. I took that as a documentation gap and went
looking for the names.

It is not a gap. Re-running `recover_error_codes.py` against the binary produced
**605 unambiguous and 9 category-dependent** codes, matching the page **row for
row, 605 of 605, zero differences**. The apparent shortfall is 23 small values
from a different switch arm, the 7 category-dependent codes the page already
excludes **by name in its own text**, and labels like
`case 0x6415: goto LAB_007b9116;` that share a block and carry no string -- so
the tool rightly declines to name them.

Two lessons, and the second is the one worth keeping:

- the page said "9 are category-dependent ... must not be used to label
  anything" and I read past it, which is the same docs-first failure this
  project keeps recording;
- **a count of syntactic labels is not a count of facts.** 643 `case` labels do
  not mean 643 recoverable names, and the difference was entirely explicable.

The re-run was not wasted: a 605-row table recovered through two jump tables is
now **verified reproducible** rather than assumed, which no round had done.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-second round: a composite item is a premium item with a use count

Round 321's sweep left two bounded unread regions. One turned out to be closed
already -- the academy's "third branch, NOT read" has a heading directly above
it in the same file recording that it is a refusal, so the append-only log
answers itself. The other is the note about three "created functions profiled
but not read": `0x00515340` guild, `0x004ae0c0` storage, `0x00511640` premium.

**`0x00515340` was already named** `GObjPC_HandleGuildMsg_0f1`, so the note was
two-thirds stale before this round started.

### The premium one, read

`0x00511640` handles client message `0x15f` and replies `0xb15f`:

	entry = GObjPC::FUN_0049a2f0(0x55494c31, ...)   ; keyed search of the list at +0xc
	if !CTJ_CompositeItemKeeper::FUN_00653f70():
	        refuse 0x18c6 UIIT_MSG_PREMIUM_USE_OVER
	if keeper->slot_0x1c(request) == 1:
	        CTJ_CompositeItemKeeper::FUN_00653f20()
	        reply 0xb15f

**A "composite item" is a premium item with a bounded number of uses**, and the
engine says so in its own words rather than by inference: `igobj_vtable.md`
already holds slots 177-180 as `IsQuestByCompositeItem`,
`UseQuestByCompositeItem`, **`GetRemainCountOfQuestByCompositeItem`** and
**`GetMaxCountOfQuestByCompositeItem`**. A remaining/max pair, exhausted into
`PREMIUM_USE_OVER`.

Two pieces that were already in the repo -- the vtable slot names and the error
string -- did the work; reading the handler joined them.

**The "premium" label was assigned by profile and turns out right**, which is
worth saying either way: the refusal string is what settles it, not the profile.

### What stays open, precisely

- the key `0x55494c31`'s meaning;
- `CTJ_CompositeItemKeeper`'s tick body, one of the eleven `timed_jobs.md` lists;
- `0x004ae0c0`, now **characterised rather than read**: client opcode `0x7034`,
  refuses `0x1812 STRGERR_LOCKED_BY_OTHER_ONE`, and its other three codes
  (`0x1bfc`, `0x103e`, `0x103c`) are absent from `error_codes.md` entirely.

## Three-hundred-and-twenty-first round: sweeping for cheap unread regions, and the gate surcharge is the fortress tax

Round 320's win came from a doc naming a **bounded** unread region with an
address -- about 190 bytes, and it closed a row's standing gap. That is a
repeatable shape, so this round swept every page for it: sentences claiming
something is unread AND naming an address. **Five**, one of them the one round
320 had just closed, and one already answered by a later round (the `0xc63c94`
table, settled in round 275 as burn's damage curve).

The best of the rest affects a value srrevamp ships: `teleport_network.md` had
`fee += FUN_00486390(fee, 0)` with the note *"a surcharge on top -- unread; the
siege tax by context, labelled an inference"*.

**The inference was right, and is now a reading.** `FUN_00486390` is a 36-byte
float wrapper over `FUN_004862a0`, which:

- looks the fortress up with `AQ_Siege::FUN_00456e20` from the object's
  association at `+0x148`, then reads a **short at `fortress[4] + 0x20`** --
  the `TaxRatio` a guild master sets through `FUN_0062f640`, range **-20..+20**;
- returns a negative ratio **unchanged** (`if (rate < 1) return rate`);
- returns **0** with no association, on a failed lookup, and on two membership
  tests.

Filed as `Fortress_TaxRatioForActor` and `Fortress_TaxRatioAsFloat`.

### Two readings, taken apart, meeting

`siege.md` already recorded **"a negative tax is legal"**, read off the
*setting* function's `(uint16)(ratio + 20) <= 40` bounds check. This is the
*paying* function, read on a different day from a different address, and its
`if (rate < 1) return rate` says the same thing: a negative ratio reaches the
fee rather than being floored. Neither reading knew about the other.

### What is NOT read, and is left that way

The two exemptions. By position they are the owning guild and its alliance --
and reading a meaning off a position is exactly what characterdata column 79
punished twice, so they stay an inference with the functions named
(`GObjPC::FUN_0061d280` with `FUN_005e4390`, and `GObjPC::FUN_0061d300`).

One transcription correction fell out of it: the page showed
`FUN_00486390(fee, 0)`, which is the decompiler's guess. The callee takes the
object in EAX and the actor in EBX and reads no stack arguments.

srrevamp has no fortresses, so nothing live moves -- but the teleport fee it
already ships now has its full formula written down rather than a labelled hole.

## Three-hundred-and-twentieth round: the damage pipeline, read to its end

`damage_pipeline.md` has carried the line *"stages past 17 run to `40e819` and
are not yet read"* for as long as the page has existed, and `SYSTEMS.md` repeated
it as the row's standing gap. It is about **190 bytes**. Read:

**Stage 18 is stage 17's mirror.** Stage 17 evaluates param `0xb2` (178) on the
ATTACKER through vtable slot `+0x104`; stage 18 does the identical thing with
`0xb4` (180) on the DEFENDER -- same slot, same `!= 0` guard, same multiply.

That suggests a 2x2, and suggestion is not enough, so it was checked against the
other function: `Formula_MitigateMagicalDamage` (`0x0040e830`) pushes `0xb3`
(179) and `0xb5` (181) **in the same order**.

| | physical | magical |
|---|---|---|
| attacker % | 178 | 179 |
| defender % | 180 | 181 |

All four are range 0..100, default **0**, untagged in the registry -- so inert
on every object srrevamp builds, the same shape as the player's percentage
reduction.

**Stage 19 is a ceiling of 16,777,215**, held as a double at `.rdata 0x00b46110`
and a float at `0x00b46108`, the same number in both, and both present in the
magical twin. `2^24 - 1` is the last integer a float32 still counts one by one,
which is why that number: the engine accumulates damage in a float and converts
at the end. The conversion forces truncation (`or eax, 0xc00` before `fistp`),
so a fractional blow loses its fraction rather than rounding up.

Wired as `combat.MaxDamage` / `combat.CapDamage`, with a test that also asserts
the float32 property the constant rests on -- `2^24+1` is indistinguishable from
`2^24` while `2^24-1` is not -- so the *reason* for the number is pinned and not
just the number.

**It is unreachable with today's content.** Nothing srrevamp spawns deals
sixteen million. It is here because a ceiling the engine has should be present
and cited rather than found later as a divergence, which is the same argument
the monster-rank HP scale was wired under.

After four rounds of measured negatives, this one is a positive, and it closes
the last open item on a row marked SPECIFIED.

## Three-hundred-and-nineteenth round: 437 assert-carrying functions, and none of them can be named that way

Round 318 found that the assert lever reaches `CObjCharacter` -- 12 of its 41
unnamed functions carry a string literal. That looked like the biggest naming
opening left in the client, which is at 5.1 % NAMED against 23,494 UNKNOWN. It
is not, and the measurement is worth more than the hope was.

| | |
|---|---:|
| client functions containing an assert | **458** |
| still `FUN_` or `vslot_` | **437** |
| whose expression holds a `Class::Member` or a call | 88 |
| whose expression quotes **its own** class or name | **0** |

### The control says exactly which form works

Of the 21 assert-carrying functions already named, three got their name from the
expression, and all three quote the function itself:

	GScript::SaveGameData                     <- "SaveGameData(), dwID == SCR_INVALID_VALUE"
	GlobalDataManager::...GetTIDFromObjectID  <- "CGlobalDataManager::GetTIDFromObjectID ( 0x%X )"
	Game::CObjChild__m_pGfxEttManager         <- "CObjChild::m_pGfxEttManager->GetUsedIDNum() == 0"

The rest name a variable or a different function, and did not yield a name:

	CObjCharacter::SetDefaultWear             <- "(nEquipSlot >=0 ) && ( nEquipSlot < EQUIP_VISUAL_COUNT)"
	IFSkillMastery::...SetMasteryData         <- "m_pMasteryData"

**Those three are the only instances in the whole binary.** My first pass
counted 88 candidates by matching any `::` or call in the expression -- and
reading them showed the regex had caught `m_sRegionList.size()==0`,
`ar.IsOpen()` and `FindHeight(vPos)`: containers, handles and calls to *other*
functions. Tightened to the form the control validates, the count is **zero**.

### Why this is the honest answer and not a failure

An assert expression describes **the state being checked**, not the function
doing the checking. The three that name themselves are the accident, not the
rule -- which is the same shape as this page's earlier finding that a one-part
`Name::` log label scored 0/131 while the two-part `Class::Method ` form scored
35/35.

So the lever is **spent for naming and still good for attribution**: file and
line place a function in its source file and order it against its neighbours,
which is the ATTRIBUTED tier, not the NAMED one. `naming_ceiling.md` listed the
harvest as done without saying what it was worth; now it says.

## Three-hundred-and-eighteenth round: into the client's code, and the group selection is confirmed rather than found

Round 317 said the remaining place to look was a hardcoded table in the client's
code. This is that read, and it produced one name, one confirmation, and a
fourth dead route.

**A fourth naming rule, tested and rejected first.** Of the 279 clip names with
no file, stripping a trailing `_<letter>` recovers **18**; `_<letter><digit>`
recovers 4; dropping two trailing parts recovers 0. Eighteen of 279 is not a
rule, and "does `bow_call_b` animate like `bow_call`?" is a semantic guess, so
nothing was promoted.

**The dump read.** `CObjCharacter` has 55 functions, 41 of them unnamed, and
**12 carry a string literal** -- the assert lever reaches them. One asserts
`pStrAniNew`, and that is the animation-group selector:

	weapon = GetEquipVisual(6)
	race   = charData[0x9c]
	group  = FUN_00a5a7d0(weapon.TypeID4, race)
	assert(group, "pStrAniNew")            ; CObjCharacter.cpp:0x847
	char[0x18c] = group

Filed as `CObjCharacter::RefreshAnimationGroup` (`0x00a5bd10`).

**Slot 6 is the weapon by arithmetic, not by assumption.** `EQUIP_SLOTS.md`
already records the visual array at base `0x38`, stride `0xc`, WEAPON at `0x80`
-- and `(0x80 - 0x38) / 0xc = 6`. `FUN_00a5a7d0` was likewise already recorded
as the TypeID4 -> group-name switch, in two different pages.

So the *group* half of animation selection is now **confirmed rather than
discovered**: it is a function of the held weapon and the race byte, and of
nothing per-skill -- which is exactly what srrevamp's `_weapon_group_for`
already does. Saying that plainly matters, because it also rules the group
selection out as a hiding place for the skill -> action type link.

**The link is still unfound after five routes**: derived filename (59/338), the
BSR table (57, two fewer), any skilldata column (3 %, chance), variant-stripping
(18/279), and now the group selector. `char+0x18c` is the field to watch next.

## Three-hundred-and-seventeenth round: the join ran, and three routes are now exhausted

Round 316 named a specific next probe -- a join rather than a range test -- and
said the column would fall out of it. **It ran, and it returned a negative.**

`probe_skill_action_types.gd` prints every animation entry as
`group, action type, clip path`: 276 for the China man, and the clip names are
exactly the Basic_Code derivations (`spear 26 skill_ch_spear_pierce_a`), so the
join is clean. Taking the **519** skill rows whose derived clip appears there
and checking every numeric column for that skill's own action type:

| column | rows carrying it |
|---|---:|
| 36 | 14 of 519 (**3 %**) |
| 80 | 9 (2 %) |
| the rest | <= 5 |

**No column carries it.** Column 36 leads by chance and is the documented
required mastery level -- the same false positive as round 316's range test,
now ruled out properly rather than by argument.

### And the BSR table is not the better index either

The suspicion worth testing was that srrevamp reads the wrong place: it builds
`prim\ani\char\china\man\<name>.ban` and reads the archive directly, where
the real client follows a BSR entry. **The entries point at exactly that
directory**, so the path was never wrong, and:

| | |
|---|---:|
| distinct CH skill clip names | 338 |
| present in the man BSR table | **57** |
| present on disk in that directory | **59** |
| in the BSR but not on disk | **0** |

Switching to the BSR lookup finds **two fewer** clips, not more.

### What is actually established now

The body carries **217** distinct clips against **338** skills, so sharing is
certain, and the link for the ~280 skills with no clip of their own is **not
name-based, not a skilldata column, and not in the BSR table**. Three
independent routes are exhausted.

That is worth more than it sounds: round 315 called this "82 % of skills ship no
cast animation" (wrong -- the clips exist), round 316 called it "the client uses
the wrong mechanism" (also wrong -- the mechanism and the path are both right),
and only now is the honest statement available. **The mapping is not in the data
this project can reach**, so the client's weapon-swing fallback is the answer
rather than a placeholder, and stays labelled disclosed.

The remaining place to look is the client's own code -- a hardcoded table -- and
that is a dump read, not another data probe.

## Three-hundred-and-sixteenth round: skill animations are action types, and the client was using the wrong mechanism entirely

Round 315 measured that only **59 of 338** derived cast-clip names exist and
concluded most skills ship no animation. That conclusion was half right and the
half it got wrong is the important one: **the clips exist; the lookup is wrong.**

**The decompiled client contains ZERO references to the `.ban` extension.** It
never builds a clip path in code. It looks an entry up in the body `.bsr`'s
animation table by **action type** and follows the index into the animation
list. `BSR_FORMAT.md` had already noted "26 and up are skills"; counted with a
new probe on `char\china\chinaman_fighter.bsr`:

| group | entries | action type >= 26 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `default` | 92 | **74** |
| `spear` | 58 | **50** |
| `sword` | 52 | **47** |
| `bow` | 49 | **46** |

Around fifty skill animations per weapon group, **99 distinct types** across
`sword` and `default`, running 26..220. Against that, the 59 filename matches
are the coincidences -- names that happen to exist in
`Prim\Ani\Char\China\man\` -- not the mechanism.

So srrevamp's client has been asking the wrong question since cast animations
were added, and "i used a skill, no animation" is the direct consequence.

### The column is NOT settled, and the obvious probe cannot settle it

Scanning every skilldata column for values inside the 99-type set ranks
**column 36 first, at 64 % of rows**. Column 36 is already documented as the
**required mastery level**. With 99 permitted values spread over 26..220, any
numeric column scores well by chance, so the range test discriminates nothing
and **no column is promoted**.

This is the third time this session a "value falls in the right set" probe has
produced a confident false positive -- after the `0x54` descriptor's type code
and the `_CHAR` offset naming lever. The pattern is the same each time: a wide
permitted set makes agreement cheap.

**The next probe is a join, not a range test.** For the 59 skills whose derived
filename does exist the clip is known, so printing each BSR entry's action type
beside the clip it indexes gives those skills their action type directly; the
column is then whichever one carries that number on those rows.

Recorded rather than wired: the client keeps its disclosed weapon-swing
fallback until the real mapping is in hand, which is the honest state and is
labelled as such at the function.

## Three-hundred-and-fifteenth round: the skill animation that does not exist, and a listing that nearly lied

"i used a skill, no animation" (playtest 2026-09-20). The cause is not a bug in
the lookup -- it is that **most skills have no cast clip at all**.

The client builds the path
`Prim\Ani\Char\China\<gender>\<Basic_Code lowercased, level suffix dropped>.ban`.
Listing the real directory and reading its **tail** showed names like
`sword_smash_a.ban` and `sword_magic_target.ban`, with no `skill_ch_` prefix
anywhere in view -- so the obvious conclusion was that the client's derivation
keeps a prefix the filenames do not have.

**That conclusion was wrong, and the measurement caught it before the fix did.**

	current rule (keep skill_ch_, drop _NN)   540 / 2944 rows  (18.3 %)
	strip skill_ch_, drop _NN                  56 / 2944       ( 1.9 %)
	strip skill_ch_, keep _NN                   2 / 2944       ( 0.1 %)

The existing rule wins by tenfold. `grep -c "^skill_ch_"` on the listing:
**135 of 334**. The `tail -15` had shown only the alphabetical end, where the
`sword_*` names live. This is the same truncated-read mistake as round 308's
`character_schema.md`, caught this time by running the numbers before editing.

### What is actually true

Of the **338 distinct** clip names the 2,944 China skill rows derive, only
**59 exist**. Stripping the prefix as a fallback gains exactly **one**
(`skill_ch_bow_base` -> `bow_base`).

**And there is no animation column.** Every skilldata column was scanned for a
value naming a real `.ban` file; exactly one scored -- **column 5, 1,482 of
2,944 rows** -- and it is a false positive of the circular kind. Column 5 holds
the skill's **base code** (`SKILL_CH_SWORD_SMASH_D` on every level row of
`..._01..08`), which is the string the derivation already produces, so it
matched itself. Worth keeping as the better SOURCE of that name -- read rather
than reconstructed by dropping a suffix -- but it adds no coverage.

So **82 % of China skills ship no dedicated cast animation** under any rule
tried, and casting one played nothing whatsoever.

### The fix is disclosed, not recovered

The client now falls back to the weapon's own attack clip, so a cast always
shows something. That is **this project's choice**, labelled as such at the
function: what the original plays for those skills is not recovered, and the
effect layer (`.efp`) is the obvious unread place. Recorded in
`skill_fields.md` with the three tables above, so the next reader does not
re-measure it.

## Three-hundred-and-fourteenth round: the grounding audit was three features behind the code

The project's goal is that every value is **grounded with a citation or disclosed
with a proven reason**, and `docs/GROUNDING_AUDIT.md` is the page that says which
is which. Its closing section -- *"what is genuinely still assumed (summary for
the next pass)"* -- is therefore the list of everything not yet at that bar.

**It was wrong about most of what it listed.** Checked against the shipping code
rather than against itself:

| the audit said | the code says |
|---|---|
| "no dodge/crit/evade" | `PlayerCritical`/`MonsterCritical` are on the wire, and the roll is not even memoryless -- `combat/chancememory.go` implements the engine's per-actor accumulator from `FUN_00599cc0` |
| (same bullet) | `PlayerBlocked` is on the wire; a blocked hit deals nothing |
| "monster always counterattacks" | gated by `combat.Hub.CounterattackReady` since round 254 -- Mangyang 3000 ms, Gyo 2000, Yeoha 2500, each the species' own attack-skill ReuseDelay |
| "monster stats ... placeholder by intent" | MaxHP is `characterdata` col 59 and the attack range col 83's skill `'att'`, both cited in `internal/combat/combat.go` itself |
| "prices ... placeholder" | `itemdata` cols 26/31, `SellPrice < Price` on every real row |
| "flat HP" | superseded by `MaxHP = Str x 10 x 1.02^(lvl-1)` |
| "loot values ... placeholder by intent" | a **proven absence**: loot is DB-only, censused at 17 server-side tables with a test that fails if the count drifts |

That last one matters for the goal's wording. "Placeholder by intent" and
"disclosed with a proven reason" are different states, and loot has been in the
second for a while: the tables were counted and shown to be server-side. Calling
it a placeholder undersold a finished piece of work.

**What actually survives**, and is now all the section claims: the attack-combo
order, **parry and evade** (parry is recovered as ParamKeeper param 9 but nothing
wires it; the evade tags in `paramtags.go` are vocabulary only), quest objectives
(proven not to be data), and the placeholder loot item ids 500-502.

### Twice is a pattern, so this one gets a guard

This section has now rotted twice. The 2026-09-17 pass found it telling readers
the server binary was "a third-party emulator bundle, not authoritative" --
discounting the artifact most recovered values come from. This pass found it
describing a combat system three features behind the code.

`internal/systems` guards `SYSTEMS.md` against exactly this and nothing guarded
this page. `TestGroundingAuditMatchesTheShippedCombat` now pairs three claims
with three symbols: if `PlayerCritical`, `PlayerBlocked` or `CounterattackReady`
disappears the audit has become wrong, and if the audit stops crediting them the
mismatch says so. Verified by breaking it -- editing "Criticals are real and
rolled" out of the page fails the test with that sentence quoted back.

A prose page cannot be checked in general. A specific pairing can.

## Three-hundred-and-thirteenth round: a lever measured and rejected, and a "next step" that was never a gap

### The obvious use of 409 offsets does not work

Rounds 307-308 recovered every runtime column with its struct offset. The
obvious next move: name unnamed functions by the offsets they touch -- a
function reading several `_CHAR` offsets ought to be character code. It is the
first thing anyone holding that table would try.

**Measured, it scores 18 %.** Control: the 5,621 already-named server
functions, 425 of which name themselves character code (`CInstancePC`,
`GObjPC`, `CharData`, `CGObjChar`, `Char_`).

| threshold | selected | actually character code | precision | recall |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| >= 4 shared offsets | 117 | 21 | **18 %** | 5 % |
| >= 6 | 43 | 6 | 14 % | 1 % |
| >= 8 | 26 | 3 | 12 % | 1 % |
| >= 10 | 17 | 3 | 18 % | 1 % |
| >= 12 | 6 | 1 | 17 % | 0 % |

**Precision does not rise with the threshold.** That is the signature of noise:
a real signal concentrates at the top, and this does not move. The project's own
bar is the two-part `Class::Method` form at 35/35 against the one-part `Name::`
at 0/131, which was rejected.

Two attempts, and the first failure was visible before the numbers. The naive
version put `RTNavMeshDungeon` and `RTNavMeshTerrain` in its top ten -- navmesh
code has no character record. Weighting by rarity did not help, because **38 of
the 43 offsets are already used by under 1 % of functions**, so the filter
removes nothing; and the counterexample is decisive: **`__get_lc_time`, a CRT
locale routine, touches 17 of `_CHAR`'s offsets.**

**Why it cannot work:** struct offsets are not a vocabulary. Any sizeable
function touches dozens of small offsets incidentally, so the overlap measures a
function's SIZE far more than its subject. The offsets stay valuable for the
reverse lookup they were built for -- given `charData+0x86`, name the column --
which is a different question from naming the function that touches it.

Recorded in `naming_ceiling.md` so the next session does not spend a tick
rediscovering it.

### The berserk window was never an open gap

Round 312 closed the orb count and left "the ACTIVE window is still transient --
a character logging out mid-berserk loses the remaining duration" as the row's
next step. **That was my framing, and it was wrong.**

`_CHAR`'s 43 columns are now fully listed, and they carry `HwanLevel` and
`RemainHwanCount` and **no duration or expiry column at all** -- the only
time-like column is `LastLogout`. The engine cannot persist a running berserk
either. srrevamp dropping it on logout is **faithful, not a gap**, and the
absence of a column is the proof.

This is the same shape as the quest-objective finding that this project treats
as a model: *proving the data does not exist is itself a recovery*. The row's
next step is corrected to the two things actually open -- param 184's tag and
writers, and the party share, which needs party-support monsters to exist.

## Three-hundred-and-twelfth round: the key parked on evidence, and the orbs finally persisted

Two halves: one probe closed as far as honesty allows, and one shipped change
that the last five rounds' work earned.

### The lookup key, parked with a measurement rather than a shrug

Round 311 left "read what populates the container". Following it first corrected
my own reasoning: **the container cannot be keyed by that int alone.** `_CHAR`
passes only ~8 distinct values but `BindTableSchema` walks **43** column
records, so the key selects something a column *has*, not the column itself. A
per-type handler fits.

Tested on the 20 tables where keys and offsets both align: in **15 a key implies
exactly one field width** within its table. The 5 exceptions each pair a small
width with a larger one -- `{4,16}`, `{4,8}`, `{16,28}` -- which is precisely
what an **unbound struct member sitting between two bound columns** produces,
since the delta then overstates the field. So the test can neither confirm nor
refute a type id.

15 of 20 is a suggestive curve, and this project has a rule about those. It is
recorded in the TSV header with the confound named, and **not promoted**. By the
tick-budget rule it is also the right place to stop: the key's meaning grounds
**zero** values srrevamp uses, while the offsets it sits beside are done.

### The berserk orbs now survive a logout

`berserk.Tracker` carried a comment saying the count "is a DB column, but
srrevamp clears it on disconnect like a duel until the character store carries
it". Round 308's schema made that concrete: **`_CHAR.RemainHwanCount` is bound
at charData `+0x86`**, an offset verified from the decompilation and again from
raw disassembly. The engine persists it on the character row, so srrevamp does
now too:

- `character.Character.HwanCount`, mapped to `_CHAR.RemainHwanCount` in
  `character.Mapping` (it moved out of `EngineOnlyColumns`);
- an `hwan_count` column with the usual `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` migration;
- `Store.SetHwanCount`, written by **both** paths that change the count -- the
  killing blow that earns and the activation that spends five;
- `Tracker.EnsureSeeded`, restoring the stored count.

**Seeding is lazy and seed-once, and that is the part with a bug in it if done
carelessly.** A session has no single "entered the world" moment -- it resolves
a character per request -- so the seed happens on first touch. Seed-once
matters because the live count is the authority once play has started: a second
seed from a stale row would silently destroy orbs earned since. A test asserts
exactly that, and two more cover a row holding 99 or -4.

The project's own guard caught the change before I did: `TestEveryCharacterFieldIsMapped`
failed the moment the field existed, demanding it be mapped to a `_CHAR` column
or declared a divergence. It was already right that `RemainHwanCount` existed;
what changed is that it is no longer engine-only.

Still transient: the **active window**. A character logging out mid-berserk
loses the remaining duration, which is now the row's named next step.

## Three-hundred-and-eleventh round: the second integer was never a per-column code, and I withdrew it

Round 310 left one thing open and named the probe: the binder inserts into a
`std::map`, so read the value type. Following it says the question was **posed
wrongly**, and that three rounds of mine published a column that should not have
existed.

The disassembly of a single binding:

	call 0x401fc0                     ; build the column-name string
	lea  ebx,[esp+0x20]               ; EBX -> the KEY
	mov  DWORD PTR [esp+0xdc],0x66    ; the STRUCT OFFSET  (_CHAR MaxLevel)
	mov  DWORD PTR [esp+0x20],0x2     ; the key's value
	call 0x862e40                     ; lower_bound

`FUN_00862e40` dereferences `unaff_EBX` and compares it against each node's key.
So the second integer **is a lookup key**, not a datum stored per column. It
selects an entry in a container, and the binder then uses that entry's `+0x48`.

**Each table has its own container**, which is why the key can repeat:
`_CHAR` `0xd1fbe4`, `_CHARCOS` `0xd1fcec`, `_ITEMS` `0xd2042c`, `_GUILD`
`0xd2109c`. Keys are small (0..11) and **29 of 50 tables reuse one**, so it is
neither a column ordinal nor a unique id.

### And the published values were often the wrong slot

For `_CHAR` the key slot is `0x20`. The decompiler's second variable, which
rounds 308-310 recorded as the "code", was slot `0x2c` -- a different stack
location entirely. The numbers in that column were partly noise, which is why
they refused to settle into any story: round 310 measured them against widths
and against column identity and got incoherence from both. **The incoherence was
the signal, and I read it as "unsettled" rather than "wrong".**

A corrected key column could only be aligned for **26 of the 50** binders,
because the compiler keeps EBX live across some bindings and does not re-emit
the `lea`. Rather than publish a half-aligned column, it is **removed**.

### What survives, and it is the part that matters

The **offsets are untouched and are the doubly-verified artifact**: extracted
from the decompilation, then again from raw disassembly, identical across all
50 tables the assembly path covers, 403 of them, with the six single-column
binders settled by sibling agreement. Nothing in `persistence.ColumnOffsets`
changes.

**The lesson is about which half of a finding to trust.** The offsets had two
independent derivations and five controls; the code had neither, and it rode
along in the same file and the same commits because it came out of the same
parse. A number that arrives as a by-product is not evidence merely because the
thing beside it is.

Next probe, sharper than round 310's: read what populates a per-table container
(`0xd1fbe4` for `_CHAR`) and what lives at entry `+0x48`.

## Three-hundred-and-tenth round: the offsets verified from a second direction, and what the other integer is not

Rounds 308 and 309 produced three parses of the same data, two of them wrong.
After that, "the controls pass" is not enough. So the offsets were extracted a
**second time, from raw disassembly**, which shares no failure mode with the
decompiler read -- no STL reconstruction, no variable names, no assumption about
source order. Per binding the compiler emits

	mov DWORD PTR [esp+0xdc], 0x65     ; the offset  (_CHAR CurLevel)
	mov DWORD PTR [esp+0x20], 0x2      ; the other integer
	call 0x862e40                      ; std::map operator[]

and **slot A is fixed for a whole function**, so the offset slot identifies
itself by varying while the other does not.

**All 50 tables the assembly path covers are IDENTICAL to the published
offsets -- 403 of them.** `_SiegeFortress`, the table that broke round 309,
comes out of the disassembly as `0x18, 0x1c, 0x20, 0x28, 0x30, 0x34, 0x38,
0x54, 0x64, 0x65`, matching the corrected TSV exactly. The remaining six are the
single-column binders, which have too few bindings to identify a slot at all and
stay settled by sibling agreement.

### What the second integer is NOT

It is real per-column data -- its slot is fixed per function and its value
changes from column to column -- but two hypotheses are now dead:

- **Not a width.** It differs from the next-offset delta in **332 of 353** cases.
- **Not a property of the column.** Of 55 column names that appear in more than
  one table, **32 carry different codes in different tables**: `CharID` is 0 in
  one and 2 in another, `PosX` 3 and 5, `HP` 2, 3 and 6.

Its shape refuses to settle into one story: in `_CHAR` it repeats heavily
(0, 1, 1, 1, 7, 2, 2 …, density 0.39), while in `_SiegeFortress` it is a clean
near-consecutive run (0, 2, 3 … 10, density 0.91). Small everywhere -- 0 to 10.

**So it stays recorded and uninterpreted**, and the next probe is specific
rather than vague: the binder inserts into a `std::map<string, V>`; read `V` and
find where its second field is loaded. Guessing from the distribution is exactly
what characterdata column 79 punished twice.

### Recorded before it was re-derived

`FUN_00972b40` is already named `Database::BindTableSchema` and already carries
an annotation saying it fetches column metadata over ODBC, compares each `0x54`
record's declared name with `CompareStringA`, and on a match writes **the ODBC
column index into `+0x30` and a skip flag into `+0x34`**. That is the runtime
half of the structure rounds 305 and 306 read, and opening it first would have
supplied it.

## Three-hundred-and-ninth round: the structural check was too weak, and 18 offsets were wrong

Round 308 published 409 column offsets and justified them with a structural
check -- *no two columns of one table may share an offset* -- writing that
"controls confirm the cases you thought of; a structure constrains the ones you
did not". **The structure was too weak, and 18 of the 409 were wrong**, across
eight tables.

`_SiegeFortress` is the case that breaks it:

	FortressID   off=0x0   code=24
	GuildID      off=0x2   code=28
	TaxRatio     off=0x3   code=32
	Tax          off=0x4   code=40
	...
	IntroductionModificationPermission  off=0xa  code=101

The left column is `0, 2, 3, 4 ... 10` -- a **column index**. The right is
`24, 28, 32, 40, 48, 52, 56, 84, 100, 101`: ascending, with strides 4, 4, 8, 8,
4, 4, **28**, 16, 1 -- a struct, including a 28-byte string for `Introduction`,
the same width `_CHAR`'s names use. The offsets and the index had been swapped.

**Neither guard caught it.** The `_CHAR` controls passed, because `_CHAR` was
parsed correctly. The no-duplicates check passed, because **a column index has
no duplicates either**. Round 308's rule -- take the more *distinct* of the two
integers -- cannot separate them: an index is perfectly distinct.

### The discriminator that does work

An offset is distinct **and sparse**. A column index is a near-consecutive run,
so its density (`distinct / (max - min + 1)`) approaches 1; a struct offset set
is far sparser. `_CHAR` spreads 43 columns over `0x20..0xf2` -- density 0.20.
`_SiegeFortress`'s index: 10 values over `0x0..0xa` -- density 0.91.

Re-run: **409 offsets, zero duplicates, and all seven controls pass**, the two
new ones being `_SiegeFortress` `FortressID` 0x18 and `Introduction` 0x38 --
added precisely because they are the case the `_CHAR` controls could not see.
A test now also fails any table whose offsets come out denser than 0.8.

### Six columns resolved by agreement rather than by statistics

The single-column binders (`_INVENTORY`, `_CHEST`, `_INVCOS`, `_GUILDCHEST` and
two more) bind one column, `Slot`, so there is no distribution to test and the
honest first answer was *unresolved*. They are settled a different way: **all six
sibling functions bind `Slot` at `0x18` with code 2**. Six independent
agreements, matching `db_columns.md`'s note that these tables reuse a sibling's
schema.

### What this says about controls

Three parses of the same data now: the first two passed every control they had
and were wrong. A control can only fail on a case someone already imagined, and
both times the imagined case (`_CHAR`) was the one being parsed correctly. What
found both defects was a property the data must have *in general* -- first
uniqueness, then sparsity -- and the second only after the first proved
insufficient. **The right response to a structural check passing is to ask what
it cannot distinguish.**

The second per-column code remains recorded and uninterpreted: it differs from
the next-offset delta in 332 of 353 cases, so it is not a width, and no use-site
has been read. `FUN_00862e40`, which round 308 called "commit the binding", is
in fact a `std::map` lower_bound -- the binder is building a
`map<string, {offset, code}>` and that call is its `operator[]`.

## Three-hundred-and-eighth round: the offsets, and a parse that passed its controls while being wrong

Round 307 named every runtime column and left the other half of each binding
unread. It is right there:

	FUN_00401fc0("Strength", 8);   // the column name
	<offvar>  = 0x74;              // the struct offset
	<typevar> = 2;                 // a second code
	FUN_00862e40();                // commit

**All 409 columns now have an offset**, in `db_bind_offsets.tsv` and
`persistence.ColumnOffsets`, with `OffsetOf` and `ColumnAt`. The reverse lookup
is the direction this project keeps needing: an offset turns up in a decompiled
function and the question is which column it is.
`ColumnAt("_CHAR", 0x86)` answers `RemainHwanCount`.

### The first parse passed both controls and was still wrong

Taking the first assignment after each name gave `Strength` = `0x74` and
`RemainHwanCount` = `0x86` — **both controls, exact, from unrelated earlier
rounds**. It was wrong anyway. `PosX`, `PosY` and `PosZ` all came out at
**`0x5`**, because those three emit the two assignments in the opposite order,
and their "type codes" were 152, 156 and 160 — which is `0x98`, `0x9c`, `0xa0`,
a consecutive 4-byte float triple, the offsets themselves.

What caught it was not a control but a **structural** check: *no two columns of
one table may share an offset*. Two pairs collided out of 409, and both were
this. Controls confirm the cases you thought of; a structure constrains the ones
you did not.

The fix identifies the offset variable per function as **the one whose values
are distinct across bindings** — an offset cannot repeat, a type code must.
Re-run: 409 offsets, **zero collisions**, and PosX/PosY/PosZ land on
`0x98`/`0x9c`/`0xa0`.

### Round 307's `Name*N` guess is now proven, with its stride

`_ITEMS` `MagParam` is **twelve** rows at `0x60, 0x68 … 0xb8` — an exact 8-byte
stride — sitting immediately after `MagParamNum` at `0x58`. A count field in
front of the array it counts. Two extractions made on different days by
different scripts agree on the multiplicity, and a test now asserts that
agreement for every `Name*N` column.

### The second code is recorded and NOT interpreted

It is tempting to call it a type or a width. It is not a width: sorting each
table by offset and taking deltas gives code 2 a width of 4 in only **71 of 121**
cases and code 0 in **56 of 66**, and codes 84, 100 and 1000 exist. No use-site
has been read, so the TSV carries the number and says plainly that it means
nothing yet.

## Three-hundred-and-seventh round: 409 columns, and 54 was never the table count

Round 306 ended by noticing the `DB_Bind__<TABLE>` family in passing. It is the
lever that closes a bullet standing in three separate pages: `persistence.md`'s
"**column layouts for any of the 35 runtime tables**", `academy.md`'s "a
complete column list for any of the four tables", and the reason `db_columns.md`
could not give one -- **the schema string pool is deduplicated, so it records
only the names a table INTRODUCES**, and seven tables introduce none at all.

Each binder declares its table and then every column **by name**. One pass over
all 56: **409 columns across 59 tables**, now in
`docs/protocol/db_bind_columns.tsv` and `persistence.BoundColumns`.

**The control, run before the sweep was believed.** `_CHAR` is the one table
with an independent answer -- `character_schema.md`'s 42 names, from the pool.
The binder gives 43, and the difference is exactly right:

	in binder, not in doc:  CharID     (the key, which the pool attributes
	                                    to whichever table introduces it first)
	in doc, not in binder:  (nothing)

A test pins it, because `_CHAR` is the only one of the 59 that can be checked
against a second source.

### The first extraction was wrong, and said so loudly

Reading only inline `FUN_00401fc0("Name", len)` literals found 346 columns and
reported **five tables as having none** -- `_INVENTORY`, `_CHEST`, `_INVCOS` and
two siblings. That looked plausible, because `db_columns.md` describes exactly
those tables as "reuses a sibling's". It was wrong: the names are passed as
**pointers into the schema pool** (`FUN_00401fc0(&DAT_00b11d70, 4)`), which the
regex could not see. Resolving them through the PE gives 409 and no empty table.

A zero that agrees with something you already believe is the most expensive kind.

### `Ally*8`: names the binary builds rather than stores

`_ALLIEDCLANS` came out as `Ally` repeated eight times. The binder emits the
base name, walks it for length, and calls `FUN_0041f4a0` to append an index --
so the real columns are `Ally1..Ally8`. `_GUILDWAR` and `_ITEMS` do the same.
**This is why the pool lists `_ALLIEDCLANS` as introducing ONE name for eight
columns**, and the TSV marks the pattern `Name*N` rather than pretending to
eight distinct strings.

### And a wrong assumption that turned into the round's best finding

The first version of the guard test asserted that every bound table is a table
the pool knows. It failed on five: `_OpenMarket`, `_ShopItemStockQuantity`,
`_RentItemInfo`, `_ChestInfo`, `_BindingOptionWithItem`. Not an extraction
defect -- **none of the five appears anywhere in the 310-string pool**, and the
reason is visible in the binder: they declare the table name as an **inline
literal** instead of a pool pointer, and a literal is never registered.

`_ChestInfo` corroborates from two directions: the warehouse work had already
cited its binder at `0x8586e0`, and this sweep found `DB_Bind__ChestInfo` at
that same address without being told.

**So `db_columns.md`'s "54 table names" is not the runtime table count.** The
binders say at least **59**. The test now records the five with the reason
rather than asserting the thing that was false.

## Three-hundred-and-sixth round: a dig that re-derived a recorded page, and the pointer that sent it there

**Most of this round confirms what `docs/protocol/db_columns.md` already says,
and that is worth stating before anything else.** The dig went after the
per-column schema behind `FUN_006b1a80` and recovered, in order: that the
records are `0x54` bytes, that the classes are `CDBTable`/`CDBRecord`/
`CTableKeeper` (RTTI), that `ODBC32.dll` is imported, that binding happens **by
column name**, and that the binder family is `DB_Bind__<TABLE>`. Every one of
those is on that page, or in `NameDBBinders.java`, or in `character_schema.md`.
`ls docs/protocol/` was run at the start of this session; `db_columns.md` was
never opened, while the dig was explicitly about a *column schema*. Fifth time.

**The genuinely new part is why the dig happened at all.**
`refobj_binary_format.md` ended its "this is a dead end" section by naming the
next route:

> The route for a type-specific column is the **per-column schema** the stream
> carries ... That is where a type-specific index lives; counting reads is not.

`db_columns.md` had already read the *other end of that same structure* and
titled the result **"Why the names are in the binary and the indices are not"**.
`Database::FUN_00972b40` walks the identical `0x54` records and binds each **by
name**, comparing the declared string against the name ODBC reports for the live
result set. The ordinal is a **database** column number filled at runtime. The
server never sees a text column: it reads SQL rows, not the client's `.txt`
files.

So one page's recommended next probe was another page's proven dead end, and the
tick was spent walking it. Same defect as round 304, where `durability.md` sent
readers at a 7,052-byte function while the section above named the 3,071-byte one.

**All three routes to a type-specific TEXT column are now recorded dead ends**,
which converts a vague open probe into a proven negative:

1. counting the deserializer's field reads -- item is 7 short of its text columns, char 24;
2. the per-column schema -- binds by name against ODBC, holds no text index;
3. the client side -- `Client_LoadRefDataFile`'s own annotation says per-type
   parsing lives behind it in a per-type manager, "which is why the client side
   of the characterdata column map was a dead end".

**One small real merge.** Two rounds read opposite ends of the `0x54` record and
neither had the whole thing; it is now in one table:

| offset | meaning | read in |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x04` | declared column name (`std::string`, SSO) | `db_columns.md` |
| `+0x18` | SSO length flag, `< 0x10` means inline | `db_columns.md` |
| `+0x24` | byte width, added to the row cursor to skip | round 305 |
| `+0x30` | column ordinal, **1-based** | round 305 |

**And one probe failure to retract.** Round 305 reported "zero ODBC in the
server" from a grep for `SQLFetch|SQLExecDirect` in the decompiled bodies.
`ODBC32.dll` is in the import table; the dump simply does not name the thunks.
`db_columns.md` had already written "an ODBC import" months of rounds ago. The
grep was a fact about the grep.

## Three-hundred-and-fifth round: 250 names that were filed and still did not exist

Round 302 ended on "a name that is not in the applier's input does not exist,
however thoroughly the function was read", and filed four names into
`recovered_names.tsv`. **All four are still `FUN_` in the dump.** So is a great
deal else:

| | |
|---|---:|
| server rows in `recovered_names.tsv` | 2,079 |
| names actually present in the dump | 1,828 |
| **filed but still `FUN_`** | **250** |

**Because filing is not applying.** The dump was built **2026-09-18 21:48**; the
TSV was last changed **2026-09-20 10:22**. `re_tick.sh` rebuilds when the
*Ghidra project* changes, and `ApplyRecoveredNames.java` is the only thing that
writes names into it -- so a row added to the TSV touches nothing at all until
that applier is **run**. `docs/RE_LOOP.md` has the recipe and even warns that
"a name that is only in a commit message does not exist"; the next link in the
same chain was missing. Round 302's lesson was necessary and not sufficient.

**Applied this round:** server `applied 264, forced 0, reowned 42, failed 0`;
client `applied 7, failed 0`. `PROJSTAMP` cleared on both dumps so the tick
rebuilds them, which it is now doing.

### There are TWO name sources, and nothing knew it

`client/tools/ghidra/ApplyKnownNames.java` carries a second, hardcoded table:

- **191 names**, of which **152 exist nowhere else**;
- 39 addresses appear in both files, and **34 of those disagree**.

Round 302's census measured prose against the TSV alone and called names
"absent"; round 303's `TestProbesSpellFunctionsByTheirRecoveredNames` read the
TSV alone too. **Both had an incomplete denominator**, and merging the sources
immediately caught a row the single-source test could not see: SYSTEMS.md spelled
`FUN_0059c4e0` while the Java table has named it `Mastery_LevelUp` since
2026-09-18. `internal/systems` now merges both, and a new test forbids the two
files from making different claims about one function.

### Adjudicating the 34, and a correction I nearly shipped

Most are one subject in two spelling eras (`GetSingleton_00d6a950` against
`GetSingleton_COverlappedJobMgr`), and those are listed explicitly rather than
pattern-matched away. Five were real disagreements of the form
`Ref*_ExtractData` (TSV) against `Ref*_<verb>` (Java), settled by a mechanical
discriminator: **only a row deserializer calls the column skipper**
`FUN_006b1a80`. Three call it 4, 1 and 3 times and are deserializers, so the
TSV wins and the Java names are corrected in place -- their richer
*descriptions* are kept, because a parser that validates as it reads is both
things at once.

**The fourth nearly went the wrong way.** `0x00427050`: the Java table says
`LoadGainRates`, the TSV `LoadServerConfig`. It calls the skipper zero times,
and a grep of its quoted strings returned exactly four -- "Individual Exp Gain
Ratio", "Party Exp Gain Ratio", "Item Drop Ratio", "Gold Drop Amount Factor" --
which names `LoadGainRates` so neatly that the TSV row was rewritten to match.

That was wrong. The row's own existing description, from round 258, lists
**25 keys**: `MONSTER_AGGRO_LINK_DECREASE_RATIO`, `HwanGainFactor`,
`PCSpeedRatio`, `GiantMonster_SpawnRatio`, `SET_FEE_RATE`, and more. They are
passed to `ServerConfig_Get` **in ECX**, so a grep for quoted strings inside the
function cannot see them. **The probe saw 4 of 25 and the four it saw were all
rates.** `LoadServerConfig` is correct and the *wider* name; the edit is
reverted and the near-miss is recorded in the test's own adjudication list.

It also corrupted the row: the long description was written into the status
column, pushing `reading` out. Caught by reading `git diff` before committing,
which is the only reason this is a paragraph and not a defect.

### Two were unresolved; the rebuilt dump settles them

`0x006a6660` and `0x006a94a0` were measured *while the rebuild was deleting the
dump underneath them* and returned zeroes that mean nothing. Re-measured against
the finished dump they call the skipper **3** and **6** times, so both are
deserializers and the TSV is right on all five. The Java names are corrected.

**The apply is verified, which is the claim this round rests on:**

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| TSV server names present in the dump | 1,828 | **2,078** |
| filed but still `FUN_` | **250** | **0** |

`verify_recovered_addresses.py` over the rebuilt dumps: 2,421 rows land on a
function **start**, 0 interior, 0 wrong-binary, and the single `outside` is the
recorded gap (`0x587260 SkillAction_Stance`). The zeroes that meant nothing
were the same failure as the other two probes this round -- a clean number
taken from an artifact that was not in a state to answer.

### And the coverage number this project quotes was stale

With the dumps rebuilt, `SymbolReport.java` -- the project's own tool, same four
tiers -- gives:

| tier | server (2026-09-17) | server (now) | client (was) | client (now) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NAMED | 1,825 (5.3 %) | **5,355 (15.7 %)** | 1,285 (3.0 %) | **2,219 (5.1 %)** |
| SLOTTED | 5,617 | 2,579 | 5,136 | 4,349 |
| ATTRIBUTED | 14,473 | 14,300 | 13,565 | 13,500 |
| UNKNOWN | 12,198 | 11,973 | 23,474 | 23,494 |

**The apply is not what moved it.** 264 names is a small part of a 3,530 rise.

**Three probes lied this round** (the string grep, the skipper count against a
