## Three-hundred-and-fourth round: every repair was half again too dear

SYSTEMS.md named `RefObjItem::ExtractData` (7,052 bytes) "the most valuable
function left", blocking two rows: alchemy's packed reinforce rates and
durability's repair price basis. **It blocked neither.** Alchemy's rates were
read in round 262. And the price basis is at `refRecord+0xa4`, which
`durability.md`'s own "Which half of the record, settled 2026-09-17" section had
already proven is written by **`RefObjCommon_ExtractData`** -- a different
function, `0x006a3090`, 3,071 bytes, an eighth the size. The page said the
answer cost 7,052 bytes of counting while the section above it said where the
answer actually lived.

One run of the already-validated `client/tools/re/fields.py`:

	field 28  ->  +0xa4    the price basis
	field 29  ->  +0xa8    the flat restore cost

**And the answer was off by one from what srrevamp shipped.** Deserializer
fields are 1-based over the row; text columns are 0-based. So `+0xa4` is
itemdata **column 27**. The exporter had `fRepairCost = 28`, which reads
`+0xa8` -- the adjacent restore cost, which the authored data sets at **1.5x
the basis**. Every repair srrevamp quoted was half again too expensive. The
Copper Sword is **198** at column 27 and **297** at column 28; srrevamp charged
297.

**Four disjoint anchors fix field k to row field k**, and the sharpest is this
project's own prior work:

| anchor | fields | the row |
|---|---|---|
| five string reads | 3-7 | CodeName, ObjName, OrgObjCodeName, NameStrID, DescStrID |
| `DecayTime` (round 227) | 14 | 10,000 ms -- which this project already calls **column 13** |
| stride-8 requirement pairs | 33-40 | the four `(dword, byte)` pairs, **columns 32-39** |
| five asset paths | 53-57 | `.bsr`, `.bsr`, `.ddj`, `xxx`, `xxx` |

`refdata.Item` records "field 14 ... column 13" **four fields below** the
`RepairCost` comment that equated field 28 with column 28. The struct
contradicted itself, and the DecayTime half was right all along.

**Why a 1.5-ratio pair cannot be separated by arithmetic, and what did separate
it.** Any test that feeds one number as "the basis" passes, because
`fullRepair == basis` is an identity of the formula, not a fact about the
column -- `TestFullRepairCostsExactlyTheBasis` had been passing on the wrong
column for three days and could never have caught it. What discriminates is the
predicate a *repair* basis must satisfy, measured across the whole real table:

| | count |
|---|---:|
| durable items with a non-zero column 27 | **13,949** |
| durable items with a zero column 27 | 12 |
| **non**-durable items with a non-zero column 27 | **0** |

Not one unrepairable item carries a basis, and the twelve exceptions are a
single coherent set: the `_SUPER` `HEAVY_07` armours, both genders, all six
slots, durability 9000/9999, vendor price 0 -- gear that never needs repair.
Column 30 is 0 for every weapon, which kills the alternative pairing outright:
were `+0xa4` column 28, the flat restore cost would be a constant zero.

**Wired**: `fRepairCost = 27`, and `TestRepairCostReadsTheBasisColumn` now
pins the column by giving the two neighbours different values -- verified to
fail on 28 and pass on 27 before being trusted. Suite green.

**The round-303 note, earning itself immediately.** That round tested
SYSTEMS.md's table rows for probes naming closed work. This entry's stale probe
was in the **prose beneath the table**, which no test covers -- and it had been
pointing every reader at a 7,052-byte function for a value that was never in
it. Same rot, one paragraph outside the fence.

### The same derivation elsewhere: audited, and clean

`fRepairCost` was not the only exporter constant derived by counting
`RefObjCommon_ExtractData`'s field reads, so the others were checked against
real data before this round closed:

| constant | column | what the data holds | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fCanTrade` 16 / `fCanSell` 17 | 16, 17 | 0/1 flags (19,017/2,535 and 21,059/493) | correct |
| `fCanDrop` 19 | 19 | the **bitmask**: 255, 223, 192, 128, 1, 0 | correct -- **WRONG, corrected in round 494** (RE_COMPLETION.md): the data signature matched column 19, but the parser stores 19 only for bits 12/13 and folds CanDrop from column 20; a matching signature is not a use-site |
| `fMaxStack` 57 | 57 | stack sizes 5000/2500/1000/10/5/3 | correct |
| `fSetID` 62 | 62 | 45 small set ids | correct |

**The off-by-one was isolated to the repair basis, and the audit says why.**
Every constant that survived had been cross-checked against a *discriminating*
data signature -- `fCanDrop`'s comment predicts 255/128/223/192 and the column
holds exactly those; `fSetID` was joined to `refsetitemgroup.txt` and matched
360 of 360 rows where a wrong column scored ~25 %. `fRepairCost`'s only check
was `fullRepair == basis`, which holds for any number at all.

So the failure was not "counting fields is unreliable". It is that **a check
which cannot fail is not a check**, and it was the only one of the five without
a signature that could tell a neighbour apart.

### Re-running round 298's bullet sweep, and two probes that were worthless

Round 298 swept every *Not recovered* bullet (13 pages, 46 bullets, 3 stale)
and said to repeat it "after any run of rounds that closes items". Rounds
299-304 closed several, and round 304's own stale bullet is one that sweep had
missed -- so the re-run was owed. **13 pages, 37 live bullets.**

Round 298 asked *does the page already hold the ANSWER?* Round 304's defect
needed a different question -- *does the page already name a CHEAPER ROUTE?* --
because `durability.md` did not contain the column; it contained the fact that
`+0xa4` belongs to a 3,071-byte function rather than the 7,052-byte one the
bullet sent readers to.

**Two probes were built and both were worthless, which is the part worth
recording:**

1. Matching bullets against sections headed `round N` returned **zero hits**.
   It was tested against round 304's own bullet and scored **0** -- the section
   that held the answer is headed *"Which half of the record, settled
   2026-09-17"*, which names no round. A probe that cannot see the one defect
   you know about cannot certify the absence of others.
2. Widening the heading test to `settled|recovered|READ|<date>` then matched
   **27 pairs** -- every bullet against *its own* section, because the heading
   "Not **recovered**" matches the widened pattern. Twenty-seven findings, all
   of them the probe reading its own reflection.

The third probe excludes not-recovered headings, and was validated before it
was believed: it fires on round 304's bullet, naming the exact section that
held the answer. Across all 37 live bullets it returns **zero**.

**So the negative is worth something this time.** After 299-304, no live bullet
on any protocol page is answered, or cheaply routed, by its own page. Round
298's three and round 304's one were the whole population.

## Three-hundred-and-third round: the tracker that cannot rot, rotted

`docs/SYSTEMS.md` is this project's completion tracker, and its header says it
"cannot rot the same way without the build going red." It had rotted. Not in a
way any of its seven tests could see, because every one of them asks whether a
row is **well formed** -- does the spec document exist, is a next probe present,
does the headline match the table -- and none asks the question that matters:
**is the probe still open?**

The Pets and COS row read, as its live work queue:

> the five switch cases in `GObjPC::FUN_004fcef0` are not mapped to COS kinds,
> and the hunger gauge (`HGPFULL_NODRINK`) is named but unread

Both were answered. `pets.md` carries them as struck-through bullets under its
own "Not recovered" heading -- the switch cases in **round 289**, the hunger
gauge in **round 300** -- and `recovered_names.tsv:381` has named `004fcef0`
`GObjPC::CheckCanSummonCOS` since the former. The tracker was contradicting its
own spec document, and had been for four rounds.

**The sweep.** Two mechanical rules over all 34 rows:

| rule | rows caught |
|---|---|
| probe spells `FUN_<addr>` for an address `recovered_names.tsv` names | **3** (Teleport, Berserk, Pets) |
| probe calls something unread that its own spec marks recovered | **1** (Pets, twice over) |

The three `FUN_` rows are a milder defect than the Pets contradiction and worth
separating. Teleport's and Berserk's prose *describes the reading in detail* --
"the teleport-use handler `FUN_00513590` compares the link's second word to the
character's gold" -- it simply kept the anonymous spelling for a function the
project had named. Stale spelling, not a stale claim. It still matters: round
301's emitter sweep listed `GObjPC::FUN_004a9050` as unnamed while
`ground_items.md` had read it in full, and round 302 spent itself reconciling
that. A `FUN_` token in a summary sends the next session to re-derive.

**Both rules are now tests**, and neither was called a guard until it was seen
to fail on the real defect: `git checkout docs/SYSTEMS.md`, run, five spelling
failures and two contradiction failures; restore, run, green.

**Two false positives, both kept as comments in the test, because each is the
project's own prose habit and a checker that flagged them would get silenced.**

1. A fixed 120-character window flagged my *own replacement text*: a recovered
   token (`item[0x2a0] * 100`) sat 110 characters before the word "Unread",
   which introduced an unrelated list. The window is now the **clause** -- split
   on ". " and "; ", never a bare period, which would cut `1..5` and
   `alchemy.Rate`.
2. The Skills row says `'efr'` "is **no longer unread**". That sentence is the
   tracker working exactly as designed, so negations ("no longer", "not",
   "never") are excluded explicitly.

**What this says about the wider ledger.** The lesson is the same one round 302
ended on, pointed at a different artifact. There, a name that was not in the
applier's input did not exist however thoroughly the function had been read.
Here, **an answer that was not written back into the tracker is not an answer
the next session can find** -- it is a question, still queued, in the one file
whose job is to say what is left. Round 289 and round 300 both did the reading
and both updated `pets.md`; neither updated the row that points at `pets.md`.
The reading is not the deliverable. The reading, filed where the next reader
looks, is.

## Three-hundred-and-second round: names this project had already earned and never filed

Round 301's emitter sweep listed `GObjPC::FUN_004a9050` among its unnamed yield. `ground_items.md`
has read that function **in full** -- `GObjPC::CheckCanPickUp`, its `CanPick` slot, its range
limits, its ownership rule. The name existed; it had just never been written into
`recovered_names.tsv`, which is the file the Ghidra applier consumes. So it never reached the
dump, and every sweep since has counted the function as anonymous.

**The sweep.** Mining `` `Class::Method` `` beside `` `0x…` `` across `docs/`: **160 addresses
named in prose, 39 absent from the TSV.** Verified against the dump: 9 are already named there
(correctly absent -- the file is for names the dump lacks), **4 are not function starts at all**,
1 is a false pairing, 5 are contradictions, and **4 were genuine gaps and are now filed** --
`CGItemEquip::CheckEquipRequirements`, `GObjPC::CheckCanPickUp`,
`CMainProcess::ParamRegistry_Register`, `ReferenceData::RefItem_ReadTypeIDs`.

**A third of the plausible candidates were wrong, and each needed checking.** `0xb45b44`
"named" `CGStorage::CheckRentalItemValidity` is a float constant -- 10.0, the pick-up range this
very lane read two rounds ago. `party.md` says "…`CParty::CheckCanCreate`, and hands the byte to
`0x5be280`": the address is the **callee**. `0x410110` took `Formula_SkillPhysDamage` from a
neighbouring line when it is `Formula_ExpRewardForContributor`. A regex over prose proposes and
the dump disposes -- which is the only reason the filed count is four rather than nine.

**And three contradictions, recorded rather than resolved.** Prose says
`AQ_StorageUpdater::DoWork` where the dump's RTTI says `AQ_StorageUpdaterForPacakageItem::DoWork`;
prose puts `CGObjSiegeStruct::CanRepair` at `0x483e80` where the dump says
`CGObjCOS_Summoned::CanRepair` **and a separate `CGObjSiegeStruct::CanRepair` exists at
`0x4cecd0`**; prose calls `0x4a9fc0` `CGObjChar::SetBerserk` where the dump says
`CGObjCOS_Summoned::SetBodyMode`. The last is not a disagreement about the code -- berserk *is*
body mode -- but the shared-implementation hazard, where the class prefix names an arbitrary
member of the sharing set.

The lesson is about bookkeeping rather than reversing: **a name that is not in the applier's
input does not exist**, however thoroughly the function was read.

## Three-hundred-and-first round: the error vocabulary, swept back into the server

Round 300 closed a three-round question in one command: `HGPFULL_NODRINK` is in neither
binary, so grepping the **code** `0x18b3` found its single emitter and that was the feed path.
That is a lever, and this round measured it.

**The sweep.** Every code in `error_codes.md` taken back through the server dump: 605 codes,
489 appear, and **294 are emitted by exactly one function** -- 146 already named, **148 still
`FUN_`**. Grouped by function, that is 144 functions, 75 of them unnamed, in
`docs/protocol/error_emitters.tsv`.

**The control, and a probe that had to be fixed first.** Measuring the 146 named emitters
against their messages scored **11 %** -- and the number was wrong. The tokeniser split
`UIIT_MSG_FLEAMARKET_ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_GOLD` on underscores but left
`CFleaMarket__SellFMarketItem` whole, so a perfect semantic match shared no token. Splitting
CamelCase took it to **58.9 %**. An 11 % result would have thrown away a working lever, and it
is the third time this session a number had to be checked before it could be believed.

**And 58.9 % is a floor, not the agreement.** The remaining "misses" are mostly right:
`CanBeEquipedAt` raising `HIGHER_STRENGTH_REQUIRED`, `CheckCanUse` raising
`CANT_PETSUM_HIGHLEVEL`, `OfferItemToPartner` raising `NOT_ENOUGH_OPPONENT_INV_SPACE`. The
message names the **refusal**, not the function.

**So it attributes and does not name** -- the same verdict the file-attribution lever got in
round 282, and for the same reason. Turning 148 refusals into 148 names would be exactly the
fabrication `naming_ceiling.md` records the one-part log label nearly causing.

**The value is the grouping.** 35 unnamed functions raise more than one code, and the
convergence says what they do: `004a9050` raises both `CANNOT_BE_PICKED` refusals, `00617360`
the three currency ones, `00617f70` both `DEALER_DONT_TREAT_*`. That is a reading list with the
subject already attached.

## Three-hundredth round: the hunger gauge, and the tie was an error code rather than a string

Round 299 found a pet gauge with a capacity, a threshold and a penalty, and refused to call it
hunger because nothing connected it to feeding. It named the probe: the feed path writing that
field.

**The probe failed, and the reason was the interesting part.** `CGItemExpendable::vslot_327`
is not in the dump's index, and `HGPFULL_NODRINK` is **in neither binary** -- so there was no
string to grep and no function to open. The name is the client's, for an **error code**:
`0x18b3`, per `error_codes.md`. The server emits numbers, not names.

**Exactly one function emits `0x18b3`**, and it is the feed:

	local_54 = (int *)piVar4[0xd];                    ; the pet's data record
	local_58 = (float)((uint)*(ushort *)(local_54 + 0x1a) * 100)
	           / (float)_DAT_00b45f90;                ; +0x1a on an int* = byte +0x68, / 10000.0
	if (_DAT_00b462e4 <= local_58) { *local_60 = 0x18b3; }   ; >= 99.0 -> "the gauge is full"

`local_54 + 0x1a` on an `int *` is **byte `0x68`** -- the same field as the penalty test, read
through the same percentage. So the gauge **is** hunger, settled by a use site:

	field      pet data record +0x68, a ushort
	capacity   10,000 -- every test is value * 100 / 10000.0, a percentage
	full       >= 99 %   refuses a feed with 0x18b3 HGPFULL_NODRINK
	low        <  30 %   half strength on eight combat params (round 299)
	per feed   item[0x2a0] * 100, asserted into 1..9999

The restore is **per item**, out of the same `+0x2a0` strided array `alchemy.md` documents, so
there is no single rate constant to find -- which is why "its rate" read as unrecoverable.

**And a naming caveat worth more than the gauge.** The feed is **case 9** of vtable slot 327,
which this project named `SetEngagedCOSforOpenMarket` by propagation from `CGItemCOSSummoner`.
The function is a multi-case dispatcher; the propagated name describes one case and would send
a reader looking for pet feeding anywhere but there. Propagation gets the *function* right and
can get the *meaning* badly wrong, and the row now says so.

Three rounds on one field: a constant noticed in an unrelated function, a gauge described but
not named, and then the error vocabulary closing it.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-ninth round: a pet gauge, its capacity, and the half-strength penalty

Round 298 left a curated list of genuinely open bullets. This one went at `ground_items.md`'s
two, found both already answered or honestly disclosed, and fell over something better on the
way.

**The ground-item bullets first, since they cost the probes.** The despawn timer and the drop
scatter are both `own design, disclosed` in srrevamp (3 minutes, a 2-unit disc) -- which is
compliant, not a defect. Chasing the engine's scatter went through `CGItem::Create`
(`0x0048f930`), which copies the drop position from `param_4+0x20/+0x24` already computed, and
the subclass `Create`s are reached through vtables, so the spawn path is not greppable from
there. Reading `CGItem::Update` for a second threshold found only the ownership window -- and
that was **already fully recorded**, 30.0 s at `0xb45e58`. Two probes, nothing new, and the
page was right both times.

**What the second constant in that expression turned out to be.** `CGObjCOS_GoldPet::vslot_215`
uses the same `0xb45e58` in a different shape:

	(petData[0x68] as ushort) * 100 / 10000.0  <  30.0   ->  GObjPC::FUN_004d60a0()

So a pet carries a **ushort gauge at `+0x68` whose full value is 10,000**, tested as a straight
percentage against **30 %**. And `FUN_004d60a0` sets **eight** ParamKeeper params -- physical
and magical damage low and high (13-16), both flat defences (5, 6), attack rate (11) and parry
rate (9) -- to **50.0**, then flushes. The 50 reads as *half of normal* because the same
argument position writes **100.0 as the neutral** when electric shock's contribution is removed
(round 275). **A pet under 30 % fights at half strength on eight stats.**

**And what it is not called.** `pets.md` lists the hunger gauge as "named but unread", and this
is the obvious candidate. It is recorded as *a gauge with a capacity, a threshold and a
penalty* rather than as hunger, because **no writer for `+0x68` was found** and nothing ties it
to feeding or to `HGPFULL_NODRINK`. The feed path (`CGItemExpendable::vslot_327`) writing this
field would settle it.

Worth noting how it was found: not by hunting the hunger gauge, but by reading a constant that
appeared in two unrelated functions and asking what the *other* one did with it.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-eighth round: sweeping every "not recovered" bullet -- three pages contradicted themselves

Round 297 struck a stale bullet in `jobs.md` and noted that `docs/protocol` pages have no
checker watching them. One stale bullet found by accident is a reason to look for the rest.

**The sweep.** Thirteen protocol pages carry a *Not recovered* section; between them, **46
bullets**. Each was read against its own page and the corpus.

**Three were stale, and all three contradicted their own page:**

| page | the bullet | what the same page already said |
|---|---|---|
| `academy.md` | "The three 24-hour windows, as server-side values" | its own *"Where the entries are created, with their real lengths"* gives ids 8/9 = `0x15180` = 86,400 s and id 10 = `0x3f480` = 259,200 s |
| `party.md` | "What the other party flag bits mean, beyond bit 0" | its flags section: "**bit 1** is item sharing" |
| `alchemy.md` | "Which ref-record offset holds the packed rates" | §1: a 20-element strided array, `element = base + (tier + 0x15) * 0x20` |

Each is now struck with the answer and a pointer to the section that had it. The academy one is
the starkest: the body says in as many words that all three windows are *read*, a dozen lines
before the list says they are not.

**And one that looked stale and is not.** `guild.md` lists "What maintains `guild + 0x44`"
while the body has a section titled *"`guild + 0x44` is the hostile count, named by two
refusals"*. Different questions: the section says what the field **is**, and closes with "**No
writer was found** -- every access to that offset inside the guild module is a comparison". The
bullet asks who *maintains* it, and is correctly open. Reading it before striking it is the
whole reason the count is three and not four.

**Why this keeps happening.** A page's body is edited when something is read; its *Not
recovered* list is edited only if the writer remembers the list exists. `internal/systems`
guards `SYSTEMS.md` rows against exactly this rot and nothing guards these pages -- so the
failure mode is structural, and a sweep is the only thing that catches it. Worth repeating
after any run of rounds that closes items.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-seventh round: a stale "not recovered", and a procedure argument that is not the enum beside it

`jobs.md` listed **"Which of the three kinds is which job"** under *Not recovered*. Round 273
recovered exactly that -- 1 Trader, 2 Robber, 3 Hunter, from two independent labellers -- and
round 295 used it to read the job experience columns. The bullet had simply never been struck.
That is the same rot `internal/systems` exists to catch, and it is worth noting that the rot
here was in a `docs/protocol` page, which no checker watches.

**The substantive half.** `AQ_Trijob`'s two named statement-issuers were recorded with their
statements but not their arguments -- which is `persistence.md`'s standing open item. Both are
now partly traced, and one is a trap:

	ExecAddTrijobReward:  EXEC _AddTrijobReward %d, %d
	    argument 1 is NOT the job kind. It is a remap of the kind byte at +0x1c:
	        kind 1 (Trader) -> 3
	        kind 2 (Robber) -> 2
	        anything else   -> Assert_BreakIfDebugger(); return 0

That last branch is the one a formatting failure also lands on, so a kind outside {1, 2}
reaching this function is a programming error. **The statement is only ever issued for Trader
and Robber, never for Hunter.** Why Trader maps to 3 and not 1 is not read; the procedure's
first parameter is evidently its own code space.

The shape is the lesson: a procedure argument that sits beside a known enum, is the same width,
and is fed from that enum's own field -- and is still not that enum. Passing the kind byte
through would have been wrong for two of the three values, and silently.

`ExecDeleteOldTrijobData`'s single argument comes from the object's `+0x18` rather than a
literal, so the age threshold it deletes by is data and there is no constant to recover.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-sixth round: columns 3 and 4 have no reader, and the sweep lied twice first

Round 295 left columns 3 and 4 predicted by the packing at `row+0x14`/`+0x18`, with no reader
found. Sweeping every function that touches `DAT_00d6aa14` settles it: **there are none.** The
columns are real in the file and unread in the server, which is a fact about the engine rather
than a gap in the search.

**The search is the part worth recording, because it produced the right-looking wrong answer
twice.** The first sweep reported `FUN_00410f10` reading `0x10 0x14 0x18` -- exactly the
predicted col 2/3/4 triple, in a `Formulae` function, which is precisely where such a reader
should live. It is not one:

	iVar3 = DAT_00d6aa14;                  ; the singleton
	iVar1 = *(int *)(iVar3 + 0x14);        ; the VECTOR's begin
	       *(int *)(iVar3 + 0x18)          ; the VECTOR's end
	iVar3 = *(int *)(iVar1 + uVar2 * 4);   ; ...and NOW iVar3 is the row

The vector's `begin`/`end` sit at `+0x14`/`+0x18` of the singleton -- **the same two numbers as
the predicted columns**. A second sweep, rewritten to track only variables assigned from
`rows[i]`, reported `CGObjCOS_GoldPet::vslot_215` reading `0x14` and `0x18`, and that was the
same trap again: the decompiler reuses one variable for the singleton and then for the row, so
the bounds checks are attributed to the row.

Only a probe that keeps the two apart answers. Two plausible hits, both bounds checks, and the
coincidence is structural rather than bad luck -- anyone sweeping this table will meet it.

**What did come out of the sweep**, since it enumerated the readers properly: two names.
`Formulae::SumMasteryUpCost` (`0x00410f10`) walks the rows downward accumulating `+0x10`,
leveldata column 2 -- a second use site for that column beside the mastery level-up handler.
And `GetSingleton_00d6aa14` (`0x00404ca0`) is the named accessor for the singleton
`manager_singletons.md` still lists as unidentified.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-fifth round: the level record, pinned at four points, and the three jobs

Round 294 put column 1 at `+8`/`+0xc`. That made a **prediction** worth testing: if the record
is a flat 4-byte packing and `+0x1c` is column 5, then column 2 must sit at `+0x10`.

It does. `FUN_0059c4e0`, the mastery level-up handler, "accumulates the level table's
`entry+0x10`" and that field is leveldata's column 2 -- recorded in this project some time ago,
for an entirely different reason. The prediction was made from one round's finding and
confirmed by another round's, with no new reading needed.

**Four anchors now pin the layout**, each from a different use site:

	+0x08/+0x0c  (64-bit)  column 1  exp to next      GObjPC_GainExpAndLevel
	+0x10                  column 2  mastery SP cost  FUN_0059c4e0
	+0x1c                  column 5  exp unit         Formula_MonsterExpReward
	+0x20/+0x24/+0x28      columns 6, 7, 8            TrijobMgr, below

That also retires an argument by elimination: `cmd/export-leveldata` justified `+0x1c` = column
5 on the grounds that "every other packing puts a provably impossible value there". The
elimination held, and it no longer carries the weight alone.

**Columns 6, 7 and 8 are the three jobs.** `0x0060dd90` indexes the same vector with the **job**
level and picks a column by the **job kind**:

	uVar7 = *(byte *)(job + 0x1d) - 1;        ; the JOB level as a 0-based index
	cVar1 = *(char *)(job + 0x1c);            ; the job kind byte
	1 -> row[0x20]   2 -> row[0x24]   3 -> row[0x28]   else Assert_BreakIfDebugger()

Round 273 already read that byte: **1 Trader, 2 Robber, 3 Hunter**, off
`GObjPC::JobRecordKindName`, which switches on this same field. So each job kind has its own
per-level column in the very table the character curve comes from, read on the path that
maintains the job record's running total at `+0x20`. The function lives in `TrijobMgr` -- the
engine's own word for the three-job system.

This page's older note that "cols 6-8 look job/cost/gold-related" turns out to have been right
about the family and vague about the reason. It now has the reason.

Nothing wired: srrevamp models job kinds but not job levels. Columns 3 and 4 are predicted by
the packing at `+0x14`/`+0x18` and are recorded as predicted, with no reader found.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-fourth round: the pet's threshold is the character's EXP curve, column 1

Round 293 established that the pet and the character read the same per-level rows, and left the
column open. `GObjPC::GObjPC_GainExpAndLevel` closes it.

**The character reads its own exp-to-next from `row+8`/`row+0xc`, as a 64-bit pair** -- adding
to it, dividing by it with `__alldiv`, and walking successive rows to carry several levels in
one gain. `param_1[0x72c]` is `char+0x1cb0`, the row `GObjPC_SetLevel` stored. The gold pet's
`OffsetExpPoint` takes its threshold from **the same offset of the same kind of row**.

So the pet's level-up threshold is the **character EXP curve**, `leveldata.txt` **column 1** --
the value `docs/LEVELING.md` had already matched against a real level-9 character's "Next Exp"
of 17,978. Column 1 now has two independent groundings: a live character's readout, and the
server's own 64-bit field.

**The layout is anchored at both ends.** The same record's `+0x1c` is column 5, the exp unit
`cmd/export-leveldata` has cited for a while; `+8`/`+0xc` is column 1. Two offsets, one record,
each established separately.

**What it changes here: nothing, and that is the useful part.** `leveldata.Table.expToNext` is
already `int64`, so srrevamp was right by construction -- but it was right on the strength of
one live observation, and it is now right with the engine's own field width behind it. A test
pins the width rather than a number: a curve carrying a value past 2^32 must survive parsing,
because a 32-bit column would wrap silently at the high levels.

A pet system here needs no new table either -- only `ExpToNext`.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-third round: the answer withheld last round, arriving as a use site

Round 292 traced the pet's experience thresholds to a vector held by the singleton
`DAT_00d6aa14`, said `_REFLEVEL` was the obvious candidate, and refused to record it -- "that is
a resemblance, not a citation". The probe it named was the vector's fill site. The fill site did
not answer; a **use site** did.

**`GObjPC::GObjPC_SetLevel` indexes the same vector**:

	uVar3 = uVar3 - 1;          ; level - 1, a 0-based index
	iVar4 = rows[uVar3];        ; the same DAT_00d6aa14 +0x14/+0x18 vector
	piVar1[0x72c] = iVar4;      ; stored on the CHARACTER at +0x1cb0

So the vector is **the per-level row table, indexed by `level - 1`**, and the function that
sets a character's level is what reads it. The gold pet does the same into its own field and
takes the 64-bit at `row+8`/`+0xc` as its threshold. **Pet levelling and character levelling
read the same rows.**

That is the difference between the two rounds, and it is the whole method: not "140 rows looks
like leveldata", but "the character's own level-set indexes this exact vector by level". Six
call sites index it that way, and one of them is a function this project had already grounded
for another reason.

By `refdata_tables.md`'s enumeration the per-level table is `_REFLEVEL` (`leveldata.txt`),
which srrevamp already loads as `leveldata.csv` -- so a pet system here needs no new table,
only the column holding the threshold. **The link from the global to that loader is still not
traced** and is recorded as such: the rows are placed from further out than `0x0082afc0`, no
function references both the global and a `"_REF…"` literal, and `FUN_006f8950` -- the one
function that walks the vector by its static symbols -- frees the rows rather than filling
them, so it is teardown.

Waiting a round cost nothing and bought a citation instead of a guess.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-second round: the pet's threshold row, traced to a singleton and stopped there

Round 291 closed pet growth and left one thread: the per-level thresholds come from a reference
row at `this+0x1ce0`, and which table that row belongs to was not read.

**Traced as far as it goes without guessing.** `this+0x1ce0` is a pointer to one row, and two
sites set it identically -- `CGObjCOS_GoldPet::vslot_215` and `GObjPC::FUN_004d6210` both index
a vector of row pointers, bounds-checked by `(end - begin) >> 2`, and store `rows[n]`. The
vector belongs to the global **`DAT_00d6aa14`**, which `OffsetExpPoint` loads directly when it
walks to the next level's threshold. So: a singleton holding a vector of rows indexed by level,
each row carrying the 64-bit threshold at `+8`/`+0xc`.

**The singleton, which `manager_singletons.md` lists as unidentified, is now at least
described.** `FUN_007158f0` installs it with the usual "already set" assert
(`DAT_00d6aa14 = &DAT_00d16c80`); its object lies past `.data`'s raw size, in uninitialised
memory, so there is **no vtable and no RTTI to walk** -- which is exactly why the class-name
levers that work everywhere else do not reach this one. It is referenced on 961 decompiled
lines.

**And the identification deliberately not made.** `_REFLEVEL` (`leveldata.txt`) is the obvious
candidate: it is the per-level table, it has 140 rows, and 140 is the number the level-up path
guards against. That is a resemblance, not a citation. This project has twice been wrong
promoting exactly that kind of fit, and the cost each time was a value shipped backwards. The
probe that would settle it is the vector's **fill** site; a sweep for any function referencing
both `DAT_00d6aa14` and a `"_REF…"` literal returns nothing, so the rows are placed from
further out than the loader.

Four probes, one answer short, and the answer withheld rather than approximated.

## Two-hundred-and-ninety-first round: a pet levels only below its owner -- the branch I refused to guess

Round 290 read `CGObjCOS_GoldPet::OffsetExpPoint` as far as it was certain and stopped at one
branch, writing: *the decompiled boolean reads as "gain when petLevel >= ownerLevel", which is
backwards from what a pet-growth rule ought to be -- and that is the signal to stop rather than
publish.* Reading the target settles it, and the caution was right: **`0x4d653e` is not a "no
experience" return at all.** It is the level-up path.

	4d6552  call [this + 0x124]      ; the PET's own level
	4d6596  cmp  level, 0x8c         ; 140
	4d65aa  jge  <elsewhere>         ; at 140 this path does not run
	4d65b0  add/adc                  ; experience += delta, 64-bit
	4d65fb  cmp  exp, threshold
	4d6611  sub  exp, threshold      ; LEVEL UP, carrying the remainder
	4d6619  add  level, 1
	4d668c  jmp  0x4d65f1            ; and around again -- several levels in one gain

So the function's two paths are a **clamp** and a **level-up**, and the gate at `0x4d641b`
chooses between them:

| when | path | effect |
|---|---|---|
| pet level >= 110, or pet level >= the owner's | clamp | experience accumulates, held at `threshold - 1`; never advances |
| otherwise, and its own level < 140 | level-up | the threshold is subtracted per level, in a loop |

**A gold pet levels only while it is below its owner's level and below 110.** At or past either
it keeps gaining experience and stops advancing -- which is exactly why the clamp path writes
`threshold - 1` instead of discarding the gain. The rule is not backwards; the branch was.

`server/internal/cos` carries `PetLevelUpBoundary`, `PetMaxLevel` and `PetLevelsUp` with a test
pinning the strictness (`jb` is strict, so a pet *at* its owner's level clamps).

The lesson is the one round 290 banked on: when a decompiled boolean reads backwards for the
rule it claims to be, the branch target is the thing to read, not the boolean. One objdump
turned a rule I would have published inverted into the right way round.

## Two-hundred-and-ninetieth round: the growth pet is the one with an experience method

`pets.md` asked what distinguishes `CGObjCOS_GoldPet` from `CGObjCOS_SilkPet` "beyond their
names". Their **method sets** do, and no reading was needed to see it:

	GoldPet   Create GetRefObjID OffsetExpPoint ReleaseAndClear Update
	          vslot_000 vslot_215 vslot_310 vslot_311 vslot_399 vslot_402
	SilkPet   Create GetRefObjID                ReleaseAndClear Update
	          vslot_000 vslot_349 vslot_368

Only GoldPet has **`OffsetExpPoint`** -- the engine's own name for the experience-granting
method -- and it overrides four slots SilkPet does not, while SilkPet overrides two different
ones. Growth belongs to the gold pet; the silk pet has no experience method to call. Those slot
numbers are all past the 209 `igobj_vtable.md` recovered, so the `## Illegal ##` lever does not
name them.

**What `OffsetExpPoint` does, as far as it is unambiguous.** Pet experience is **64-bit**, at
the data record `+0x60`/`+0x64`; the per-level threshold is another 64-bit, read from a
reference row at `this+0x1ce0` `+8`/`+0xc` rather than from a constant; and experience is
**clamped rather than rolled over** -- on reaching the threshold the function writes
`threshold - 1` and recomputes the delta to match, so it never carries a pet past the boundary
itself. A real gain calls `GObjPC::FUN_004496e0(lo, hi)` and sends text id `0x30c9`.

**And a rule deliberately left unstated.** The gate is, in assembly:

	4d641b  cmp  BYTE PTR [esi+0x58], 0x6e     ; the level byte vs 110
	4d641f  jae  4d643a                        ; >= 110 skips the owner test
	4d642f  call [owner + 0x124]               ; the owner's GetLevel
	4d6431  cmp  BYTE PTR [esi+0x58], al
	4d6434  jb   4d653e                        ; below the owner's level -> elsewhere

A **110 boundary** and a comparison against the **owner's level** are both certain. What
`0x4d653e` does is not: the decompilation shows a second branch further down that also calls
`GetLevel`, so that target may be an alternative path rather than a plain "no experience"
return. The decompiled boolean reads as "gain when petLevel >= ownerLevel", which is backwards
from what a pet-growth rule ought to be -- and that is exactly the signal to stop rather than
publish. A rule inverted is the error this project has been burned by most.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-ninth round: the five COS kinds, and a hypothesis the item table killed

Three ticks of auditing, so this one went back to reading. `pets.md`'s first unrecovered bullet
was "what the five switch cases are" in `GObjPC::CheckCanSummonCOS` -- the doc knew cases 3 and
4 were pets, case 5 needed a guild, and one was the cart, but not which number was which.

**The selector.** The switch is on `*(ushort *)(obj + 0x80) >> 11`. A 16-bit packed type id
shifted down by eleven is how the client reads a **TypeID4** as well -- `ITEM_FORMAT.md` already
records `FUN_00a5a7d0` doing exactly that to pick a weapon's animation group -- so the cases are
TypeID4 values, not an arbitrary enum.

**Whose TypeID4, settled by measurement, and the first answer was wrong.** Taking it as the
summoner ITEM's, the COS rows of `itemdata` carry TypeID4 **1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 12** -- not a
range a five-case switch can cover. The hypothesis predicted 1..5 and the table said otherwise,
which is the whole value of asking a table instead of asking oneself. Taking it as the summoned
CHARACTER's, `characterdata`'s `TypeID3 == 3` family runs exactly 1 to 5 and stops:

	TID4  rows   the rows' own names              the case's refusal
	   1    63   COS_C_RUDOLPH, _UNICORN          STRGERR_YOU_CANT_ACTIVATE_CART
	   2    39   COS_T_LIZARD, _BEHEMOTH          the same
	   3  1260   COS_P_WOLF_001 ...               COS_CANT_SUMMON_DUPLICATE_PETTYPE
	   4    11   COS_P_MYOWON, _SEOWON, _RABBIT   the same
	   5  2100   COS_GUILD_CH_SOLDIER1_001 ...    GUILD_SOLDIER_SAME_SUMMON_LIMIT

**Two independent witnesses.** The table's code prefixes and the binary's refusal strings come
from different places and agree case for case: the cart error sits on exactly the `COS_C_` and
`COS_T_` rows, the pet error on `COS_P_`, the guild error on `COS_GUILD_`. That is what makes it
a reading rather than a correlation.

Wired into `server/internal/cos` as five constants with the three refusal-path predicates, and a
test that pins them to 1..5, one path each -- with 6, 7, 9 and 12 in the negative list precisely
because they are the real COS *item* TypeID4s that killed the first reading.

**Still not named:** what separates 1 from 2, and 3 from 4. The prefixes differ and the row
counts differ wildly (1,260 against 11), but this function treats each pair identically, so the
distinction lives somewhere this pass did not read. Recorded as a caveat on the constants rather
than filled in.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-eighth round: every recorded address, checked -- 2,415 starts and one known gap

Round 287 audited the *strings* this project quotes and said plainly what it did not cover:
numeric citations. Those are the backbone. Every row of `recovered_names.tsv` claims that a
particular function, at a particular address, in a particular binary, is the thing named -- and
`recovered_names_test.go` says in its own header that it **cannot check the addresses**, because
the dumps live on the RE box and the test does not.

So the check was written where the dumps are:
`client/tools/re/verify_recovered_addresses.py`, which classifies every row.

	start         2,415     the address is a function START in the claimed binary
	interior          0     inside a known function but not at its head
	wrong-binary      0     not a function here, but is one in the other binary
	outside           1     no function there in either dump

**The one `outside` is `0x587260` (`SkillAction_Stance`)** -- the dump gap `AGENTS.md` already
records as real code Ghidra never defined. The audit found it without being told it existed,
which is the best evidence available that the probe is working rather than agreeing.

Two of the four verdicts are always defects and the tool exits non-zero on them. `interior`
would mean a name attached to a jump target rather than a function; `wrong-binary` is precisely
the mistake the Go test's header remembers happening twice, when two rows were labelled `client`
for functions in the server dump. **There are none of either.**

`outside` deliberately does not fail the run: the dumps have gaps, so a new one means *go read
that address* before calling it wrong. The known gap is listed in the tool with its reason, so
it can be retired when a rebuilt dump defines the function rather than surviving as folklore.

The Go test's header now points at the tool and records the run, so the next reader is not told
the addresses are uncheckable.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-seventh round: are the quoted strings really the engine's words? 279 of 286, and one paraphrase

Round 286 found that a text sweep over the dumps matches **this project's own annotations**,
because the dumps carry the code and our prose about it in the same file. That is a way to
manufacture a citation without noticing, so the obvious next question is whether it has ever
happened here.

**The check.** Every double-quoted span of 8+ characters in `recovered_names.tsv`'s evidence
column -- 856 occurrences, **286 unique (binary, string) pairs** -- tested against the bytes of
`SR_GameServer.exe` and `sro_client.exe` directly, ASCII and UTF-16, verbatim and then by the
longest literal fragment between format specifiers.

	found verbatim                                        279
	found once an ellipsis or escaped quote was removed      5
	not a claimed literal (prose the extractor caught)       1
	a real defect                                            1

**Nothing fabricated.** For a project whose characteristic failure is a made-up constant
dressed as a finding, 286 quotations with no invention in them is the answer worth having.

**The one defect** is a paraphrase presented as a quotation. Seven rows for
`PayQuestRewardCatchMob` quoted "the engine's own"
`fail pay quest. because don``t have Catch Mob : ID[n] -> TARGET`, where the binary says
`fail pay quest. because don``t have Catch Mob : %d[%d] - >%s`. Someone had rewritten the
format specifiers into readable placeholders. The meaning survived the edit; the claim did not,
because those are not the engine's characters. Corrected in all seven.

**Checking the probe, as ever.** The first pass reported seven misses. Five were documentation
ellipses (`...`) and an escaped quote, which is the doc's formatting rather than a bad citation,
and one was a sentence of ordinary prose that happened to sit inside quotes. Only after
re-testing each by an unelided fragment did the count come down to one. A raw miss count would
have read as seven defects and been wrong by six.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-sixth round: swept -- one procedure in sixty-nine disagrees with itself

Round 285 found `_STRG_MOVE_ITEM` issued from three functions with three different format
strings, which raised the question it could not answer from one procedure: **how many of the
others do that**, and how many recorded signatures are one call site of several?

Swept all three call forms across the server dump. **69 distinct procedure names, and exactly
one has more than one distinct literal.** It is `_STRG_MOVE_ITEM`. The other 68 are consistent
wherever they are issued, so a signature quoted from any single call site of them is the
signature.

That closes the generalisation instead of leaving it hanging, and it scopes the previous round
properly: argument 4's width disagreement is a one-off in this binary, not a habit to expect
elsewhere. A negative, with the sweep that produced it.

**The probe threw a false positive, and it is the kind worth knowing.** The first pass reported
*two* disagreeing procedures, the second being `_ADDTIMEDJOB` with a form `(%d x12, %I64d, %d)`.
That string is not in the binary. It is **this project's own shorthand**, sitting in a recovered
annotation in the dump's function header -- `vtable slot 6. Builds ...`, written by round 274.
A regex for call literals matches the prose written *about* those literals, because the dumps
carry both the decompiled code and everything this project has annotated onto it. Caught before
the count was recorded, which is the only reason the count is 1 and not 2.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-fifth round: one procedure, three call sites, three signatures

The rule caught it before a word was written this time. Setting out to trace
`_UPDATE_USER_N_CHAR_GOLD`'s four arguments, `server_sql.md` turned out to have all four
already -- `(userJID, user gold, charID, character gold)`, the first id from the player
object's vslot at `+8`, its balance at `+0x1ca8`, the second from the vslot at `+0x380` and
`char-data +0x78`. Nothing to add, and this time nothing was published before checking.

**It also corrected round 284.** That round called `_STRG_DEL_ITEM`'s first argument "unread".
It is the **move kind**, and the same page had already decoded the byte: 2 = bag to chest,
`0x20`/`0x21` = guild chest, 10/11/12 = the gold moves. Fixed in `persistence.md`.

**What was genuinely open, from the same grep.** `_STRG_MOVE_ITEM` is issued from three
functions, and no two agree on the literal:

	AQ_StorageUpdater::MoveItemWithGold (0x45af70), twice   (%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,0)
	AQ_StorageUpdater::RearrangeItem    (0x45b5a0)          (%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d)
	AQ_StorageUpdater::MoveItem         (0x45c9a0)          (%d,%d,%d,%I64d,%d,%d,%d,%d)

`server_sql.md` quoted the first as though it were the signature. Two things follow that
matter to anyone implementing against it:

**Argument 4 is 64 bits.** One call site formats it `%I64d` and the other two `%d`, for the
same procedure and therefore the same column. A column cannot change width between callers, so
the narrow sites pass a 32-bit value into a 64-bit parameter -- the engine's habit, not a
reading of ours.

**Argument 8 is only literally `0` in one of the three.** The other two pass a value, so
quoting the `,0)` form alone reads as though the column were always zero.

A procedure's signature is not one call site. Three sites, three strings, and the widest one is
the one that tells you the column's type.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-fourth round: two levers measured shut, and the first procedure parameters

`ls docs/protocol/` first again, and it paid twice: `naming_ceiling.md` and `absence_audit.md`
between them already say what this lane keeps rediscovering.

**The coverage number this project quotes was wrong and is corrected in the repo already.**
Real naming is **5.3 % server / 3.0 % client**, not 21.7/14.8 -- the old figures counted
`vslot_NNN`, a vtable slot number, as a real name. A slot number and a module name are the same
kind of knowing: where a function lives, not what it does. (My own memory was carrying the
inflated figure and is now fixed.)

**Two candidate levers, both controlled, both closed.**

*Class attribution vs. assert file*: for the 348 functions with a class-qualified name in
`client_translation_units.tsv`, the class agrees with the assert's `.cpp` **332 times out of
348 (95.4 %)**, and the 16 misses are legitimate -- `CVBDynamic` lives in `VertexBuffer.cpp`,
`SWorld` methods in `Map.cpp`. That makes it a cross-check validating both attributions, not a
source of names.

*SQL procedure literals*: 31 functions issue a `{?=CALL _PROC}` literal, 20 still `FUN_`.
Controlled against the 11 named, the agreement is **semantic, not lexical** --
`AQ_StorageUpdater::DeleteItem` for `_STRG_DEL_ITEM` -- so the literal describes the function
without spelling its name. And `persistence.md` had already harvested all three call forms, 72
literals against this pass's 31.

**What did move** is the item `persistence.md` lists as not recovered: *the parameters of any
procedure, beyond how many there are*. Two of the 72 are now partly traced, by a rule worth
keeping -- **an argument that is also passed to a known accessor names itself**:

- `_STRG_DEL_ITEM (%d, %I64d, %d, %I64d)`: arg 2 is the call's own 64-bit item id, and arg 3 is
  a **storage slot**, because the same byte is handed to `CGStorage::GetItem` and `-1` in it
  makes the function log `Init() Failed`. Args 1 and 4 are left unread rather than guessed. The
  function also refuses unless that slot is already **empty** -- the in-memory removal happens
  first and the query follows.
- `_STRG_MOVE_ITEM (%d,%d,%d,%I64d,%d,%d,%d,%d)`: args 5 and 6 are the **source and destination
  slots**, both through `GetItem`; arg 4 is a 64-bit id; arg 8 is the literal `0`. Four of the
  eight are still unread and are not guessed at.

Two slots side by side, both through the same accessor, is what makes them a pair rather than
two unrelated numbers.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-third round: one visual per slot, and an empty slot wears clothes

The first command of this tick was `ls docs/protocol/` -- the rule the previous round's
correction put in place -- and the second line of the listing was `EQUIP_SLOTS.md`, a page that
already carried the nine visual slots, their order, the `this+0x38` array twelve bytes apart,
`EQUIP_VISUAL_COUNT == 9` from two differently worded asserts, and a pointer to the appearance
installer. Four rounds of re-derivation stopped in one command.

From that pointer, `CObjCharacter::InstallEquipVisual` (`0x00a61010`) reads plainly. **One
visual per slot, and installing replaces**: with a non-null item, if the slot's entry is already
occupied the function **calls itself with item 0** to detach the old visual
(`FUN_00a5fb90` + `ItemSet_RemoveWornSlotByItem`) before attaching the new one
(`FUN_00a609f0`, booked by `FUN_00a60080`); a completed set raises `this+0x1a0` through
`ItemSet_IsComplete`. Slots 9..12 never reach a mesh at all.

**And an empty slot is not empty.** `SetDefaultWear` fills it from a default-wear **item**,
resolved by `BuildDefaultWearTypeID` into a packed TypeID and looked up in the item table like
anything else. The archive says what those are: `clothes_00_ba.bsr` and `clothes_00_la.bsr` in
`MAN_ITEM`, ordinary item `.bsr` files each with their own mesh and `clothes_00.bmt`. A
character with no chest armour is wearing a garment, not showing skin.

**That corrects round 281's conclusion** -- and only the conclusion; its observation stands.
srrevamp really never hides body meshes. But the engine does not hide them either: the body
`.bsr`'s skin is drawn under the slot visual in both. So "we never hide" cannot be why skin
shows through our armour. What srrevamp is missing is the **default wear** -- an unarmoured slot
should show `clothes_00_*` and ours shows bare skin -- plus whatever keeps the engine's worn
geometry clear of the skin, which is still unread.

The buildable step falls out of the same read: nine visual slots, one visual each, default wear
when nothing is equipped, replace on install. srrevamp has no per-slot bookkeeping at all today.

Three names: the installer's semantics merged into its existing row, and its attach and detach
halves added.

## Two-hundred-and-eighty-first round: the nipples are geometry, not alpha

OpenSRO looked at the round-280 render and said "his nips are coming out". They are, and the
cause is not the alpha channel this lane had been chasing.

**srrevamp draws the naked body AND the armour.** `_build_assembled_character` assembles the
whole character `.bsr` -- for a China man that is nine meshes, `man_arm_lower`, `man_arm_upper`,
`man_calf`, `man_pelvis`, `man_thigh`, `man_torso_lower`, `man_torso_upper`, plus face and hair
-- and then calls `attach_item_from_archive` per worn item, which only ever ADDS meshes.
Nothing is hidden, ever. Skin and cuirass become near-coincident surfaces and the skin wins
wherever it is nearer.

That also makes round 280's armour-alpha finding a red herring for this item: those layers are
99.7-100 % non-opaque with bit 0 CLEAR, so honouring their alpha would make the clothes nearly
invisible rather than fix them.

**What the engine does instead**, found through round 279's translation-unit map -- which is the
first time that lever has paid for itself:

- `CObjCharacter::SetDefaultWear` (`0x00a5cca0`) asserts `nEquipSlot` against 0..8 and
  `nDefaultWearNum` against 0..1, so **`EQUIP_VISUAL_COUNT` = 9** -- the same nine slots
  `EquipmentNet.SLOT_HELM..SLOT_EXTRA` already uses -- and **`DEFAULT_WEAR_NUM` = 2**.
- `CObjCharacter::BuildDefaultWearTypeID` (`0x00a5c760`) builds each default part as a packed
  item **TypeID**: base `0x2c`, bits by gender and `WornArmorClass()`, then `| 0x1800` for
  index 0 and `| 0x2000` for index 1, resolved through the item table to a `pVisualData`.

So a character's visible parts are **per equip slot**, and a slot shows either its worn item or
its default wear. The archive agrees: `MAN_ITEM` carries `clothes_00_ba` and `clothes_00_la`
beside the real armour.

**Both functions were already named in the dump and in `recovered_names.tsv`** -- the guard test
refused the duplicate rows and the constants were merged into the existing ones instead. Third
time this session that checking first changed what got written.

**Not established, so not coded:** which body meshes a slot owns, i.e. what the engine hides
when a slot is filled. The mechanism is read; the mesh-to-slot mapping is not, and guessing it
would put invented geometry rules into the exact system being reported. The next read is
`CObjCharacter::FUN_00a604f0` (asserts `pVisualData`) and `FUN_00a60a90` (asserts
`GetCompoundObj()`).

## Two-hundred-and-eightieth round: the hair says 0x341, and the alpha survives

The RE tick for 2026-09-20 took the question the previous round's correction left standing --
bit 0 of the `.bmt` flag word is used by shipped code on a correlation, not a citation -- and
went at it from the data side rather than the binary side.

**The character materials are an independent family, and they agree.** Every layer in
`BMT_FORMAT.md`'s evidence table is scenery. `chinaman_fighter.bmt` has exactly two layers:
`chinaman_body` at **`0x0340`** and `chinaman_hair` at **`0x0341`**. Bit 0 separates body from
hair exactly as it separates bark from leaf, in a family that did not exist in the sample when
the rule was written.

**A hypothesis, formed and then killed by the measurement.** DXT1 is commonly said to lose its
1-bit alpha when an engine takes it as BC1 -- which would have made the flag moot and explained
the playtest's "hair looks like a solid block" in one stroke. `chinaman_fighter_hair.ddj` is
indeed DXT1. Decoding it through this project's own reader and counting: **2,136 of 32,768
texels are non-opaque, 6.52 %**. The alpha survives. The tidy explanation was wrong, and the
count is what said so rather than a look at the picture.

**So the chain is correct end to end**, which is the round's real result. The flag is read
(`LAYER_FLAG_MASK` 0x40 set, so the word is trusted; `LAYER_FLAG_ALPHA` 0x1 set), the hair mesh
names its material `chinaman_hair` and the layer is matched by name rather than by index, the
mask is intact, and `_build_foliage_material` applies a scissor at 0.5 on full-resolution alpha.
Nothing in that path explains a solid block.

That **narrows** the playtest item instead of closing it: either the report predates a fix, or
the player's dressed body takes a path the undressed material does not. A render is the honest
next step -- a picture to show a human the geometry, now that the numbers have settled what the
data says.

Bit 0 is still inferred rather than cited. What would settle it is unchanged and was already
written down: find where material+0x60 is tested. Round 279 found only its writers.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-eighth round: the state vocabulary, and a code that lies about itself

The RE tick for 2026-09-20 took round 277's leftover -- six status fields the page had never
listed -- and the answer came from a table the repo already had plus one literal per block.

**The kinds.** Every block in `Combat_ApplyStatusEffects` loads `kind << 24` into ECX before
asking the target's effect map whether the state may be applied. Reading that literal at all
23 sites gives each skill field its kind directly, with no inference: `+0x430` is 7, `+0x474`
is 25, and 13 and 16 are absent. `skill_fields.md` already held the field-to-code table, so
the six unnamed fields are `cssr`, `csit`, `cspd`, `csmd`, `cshp`, `csmp` and `tb`.

**The client names them too.** `0x7fdab0` in the client does not only pick an icon: it
carries a **label** beside each one, which this project had never recorded. The labels are
`FZ`, `FB`, `ES`, `BU`, `PS`, `ZB` and `DN` for seven of them -- *the skilldata codes in
upper case*. That makes the join direct rather than arithmetic, and fifteen of the
twenty-three agree letter for letter, at both ends of the run and throughout, so
`kind = bit + 1` is proven rather than assumed and the table cannot be off by a row.

It also confirms round 275 from the other binary: the client's own switch has **case 4 =
electricshock and case 8 = burn**, the same swap the server's slot table carries.

**And a trap worth the whole round.** The `cs*` codes do not mean what their letters say.
`cshp` applies the **MP** curse and `csmd` the **HP** curse. Two independent things agree:
the kind literals, and round 248's appliers -- bit 21 writes MaxHP and the client labels it
`CURSE_HP`; bit 22 writes MaxMP and is `CURSIE_MP` (the engine's own typo); bit 17 writes
physical flat defence and is `CURSE_PD`; bit 18 magical and is `CURSE_MD`. Anyone reading
these codes as mnemonics gets two states backwards. Read the state off its kind.

Two smaller facts fell out. **DISEASE (bit 15) is a state no skill block applies** -- it is
the gate the applier reads first, param 169. And **bit 23, `csmp`, has no case in the
client's switch at all**: a state the skill table can carry and the client never draws.

`statuseffect.States` carries code, field, kind, bit, icon and label with tests that pin the
trap and the internal consistency. One name, in the client. No shipped value changed.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-seventh round: the other half of the status application, read out of the FPU

The RE tick for 2026-09-20 took the last open piece of `status_effects.md`: the blocks after
the six elemental ones, whose "chance path is not read yet" had stood since round 249.

**They work the other way round.** The elemental states derive their duration from the
chance they rolled. These store **no chance at all** -- all seventeen write
`record+0x1a = 0` -- and compute the duration *and* the chance themselves, from two authored
values, each scaled by how far the target has out-levelled the status:

	d   = max(GetLevel() - 10*(value[2] + bonus), 0)
	dur = max(ftol(value[0] * (1 - 0.025*d)), ftol(0.5 * value[0]))   -> record+0xc
	chn = max(ftol(value[1] * (1 - 0.05*d)),  ftol(0.1 * value[1]))   -> rolled, not stored

**The decompiler cannot show this.** It collapses the FPU chain into five argument-less
`FUN_009fbb40()` calls -- the `ftol` helper -- so the sleep block had to be read instruction
by instruction from `0x590f06` to `0x590ff9`. The reading carries its own check: the x87
stack balances to empty, and each of `2.5`, `100.0`, `0.5` and `0.1` is consumed exactly
once.

So **value[0] is the duration in milliseconds and value[1] the chance**, and the two have
different falloffs and different floors: 2.5 % a level down to half, and 5 % a level down to
a tenth. The chance bottoms out first, at 18 levels over against the duration's 20 -- a
badly over-levelled target is hard to afflict but, once afflicted, keeps the state for half
its authored time.

**How far it reaches, by fingerprint rather than by reading seventeen blocks.** Counting the
constants per block across the whole function: sixteen of the seventeen (skill fields
`+0x430`..`+0x470`) have exactly one level term, one `2.5`, one `0.5`, one `0.1` and five
`ftol`s. `+0x438` and `+0x450` prefix an extra iterative term with an `imul`; `+0x474` has
no level term and neither `2.5` nor `0.5`. Those three are marked unread rather than assumed
to match.

The same sweep turned up something the page had never recorded: **six more status fields**,
`+0x460` through `+0x474`, each guarding a block of this family. What states they are is
*not* read and not guessed -- the elemental blocks could be identified by their resist
`GetParam` calls, and these have none.

`statuseffect.LevelOvershoot`, `NonElementalDurationMs` and `NonElementalChance` carry it
with tests that pin both floors at the overshoot the constants imply. No shipped value
changed.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-sixth round: a status effect's lifetime is its chance

The RE tick for 2026-09-20 finished what the previous one left open. Round 275 read the
whole state record -- interval, level, chance, factor, the per-state payloads, the source,
the active byte, the last-tick stamp -- and never found a duration. It is at `record+0xc`,
and the start stamp is `+0x64`, one field below the last-tick stamp that had been mistaken
for the whole of the timing.

**The removal test.** `AbnormalState_UpdateOwnerClear` (`0x4a4390`) walks all 32 slots each
pass and drops an active state when either the owner's mask at `pc+4` no longer holds the
record's own bit (`+0x8`) or `GetTickCount() - record+0x64 > record+0xc`; otherwise it ORs
the slot's mask word into the rebuilt owner mask and calls `applier(1, record)`. The mask is
the authority -- clearing a bit there removes the state on the next pass, which is what the
function's name has always meant.

**The duration is the chance.** `record+0xc` is written from a `CFormulae` switch
(`0x410b40`) that multiplies a u16 by a per-kind literal: 0 -> 97 ms, 1 -> 250, 2 and 5 ->
750, 3 -> 500, 4 -> 1000. The decompiler drops both arguments, so the six call sites had to
be read as assembly, and all six do the same two instructions:

	mov cx, WORD PTR [ebx+0x1a]      ; the resist-reduced chance the block just computed
	mov al, <kind>

So the single number that decides **whether** a state lands also decides **how long** it
lasts: freeze at chance 30 lasts 2.9 s, poison at the same chance lasts 30 s.

**And the kinds are slots, not bits.** Burn passes `al = 2` and electric shock `al = 3` --
the same swap round 275 recovered from the `0xc63ec8` mask table, now stated by a completely
different mechanism. That is the fourth independent agreement, and it means the two rows
round 248 had the wrong way round are settled beyond argument.

`statuseffect.DurationUnitMs`, `DurationMs` and `Expired` carry it with tests, including the
unsigned wrap `GetTickCount` needs and the strictness of the comparison (a state is alive at
exactly its duration). One name: `CFormulae::AbnormalStateDurationMs`. Where the
non-elemental states get their `+0xc` is still unread.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-fifth round: the table that was "by shape a duration" is burn's damage, and two appliers were the wrong way round

The RE tick for 2026-09-20 took the Status effects row's open item -- the `0xc63c94` word
table the elemental blocks index, which round 249 recorded as "by shape a duration table",
with the shape as its only evidence.

**It is burn's damage curve.** The table is written in exactly one place in the binary (the
`bu` block of `Combat_ApplyStatusEffects`, into the effect record's `+0x24`) and read in
exactly one place: an applier that, every 2001 ms, computes
`table[value[2]] / (1 + GetParam(8)/100) * record+0x20` and deals it through the damage
virtual. Read off the FPU run at `0x4a4720..0x4a4756`: `movzx` the word, `fdiv` the double
100.0, `fadd` 1.0, `fdivr`, `fmul` the record's float. **Param 8 is left unnamed** -- the
registry has it as 0..10000 with no tag, and nothing here earns it one.

**Chasing that read corrected round 248.** The applier reading `+0x24` is at *slot 2*, which
that round recorded as electric shock -- but only the *burn* block writes `+0x24`. The
engine settles it: `AbnormalState_DeactivateSlotAndRebuildMask` (`0x4a5660`) builds the
character's client-facing mask at `pc+4` by OR-ing, per active slot, a word from the table
at **`0xc63ec8`**, and that table is `1 << i` for all 32 slots **except 2 and 3, which are
swapped** -- slot 2 carries `0x8` (burn), slot 3 carries `0x4` (electric shock). Round 248
had aligned appliers to icons by slot number and by how plausible each param sounded; this
is the engine stating the alignment itself.

Three data-flow pairs agree with the table, each applier reading a field only its own
state's block writes: burn `+0x24` -> slot 2; electric shock `+0x28` -> slot 3, as
`clamp(100 - value[2], 0, 100)` on param 9 (parry), with **100** written back on removal, so
that contribution is a percent of normal; poison `+0x38` -> slot 4.

**Poison cannot kill.** Its tick is `loss = max(curHP - value[2], 1)`, `damage = curHP -
loss`, which is `min(value[2], curHP - 1)`; it also clears the source unconditionally, so no
poison tick is ever credited. Burn is the opposite: it can kill, and it drops the source
only when the blow would *not* be fatal -- which is how the killing tick gets attributed.

Also read: the states are a **fixed 32-record array** at `pc+0xc`, stride `0x70`, with the
applier for record *i* at `pc+0xe0c + 4*i` called as `(mode, record)` -- 0 apply, 1 tick,
2 remove -- and slot 5 (zombie) holds the shared 3-byte `return 0`, so it is a filled slot
with no behaviour rather than an unread one.

`internal/statuseffect` carries the mask table, the two damage formulas and the parry
percent with tests, including the one that would have caught the swap. Two names corrected,
three added. No shipped value changed: srrevamp still has no status-effect system, and this
is the spec for one.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-fourth round: how a timed job fires, and the getters were on the wrong object

The RE tick for 2026-09-20 took the Timed jobs row's open item -- "how a job fires. The managers
presumably poll, and nothing here says at what interval or through what" -- and the answer was
one call site away from work already done. The academy's 24-hour windows are entries in this
list, so round 273's dig had already handed over `0x411440` and the list at `pc+0x1dfc`.

**The manager is part of the character.** `CTimedJobManagerForPC` is embedded in `GObjPC` at
`+0x1dfc`; the call site reads `param_1 + 0x77f` on an `int *`, which is that byte offset. The
pet's manager sits at `+0x1ce4` of its owner.

**It is swept once a second, and the tick is the expiry test.** `CGObjPC::vslot_415` -- the PC's
periodic update, grounded at one second back in round 223 -- calls `0x6560c0` with `0x3f800000`,
which is `1.0f`. The sweep calls each job's **slot 8** with that elapsed time; a job that answers
0 is handed to manager slot 4, unlinked, and released through **slot 10**, which runs slot 9 and
returns it to the chunk allocator. So the three `__purecall` slots this project has carried as
`SlotPureA/B/C` since they were counted are `Tick`, `Release` and -- slot 12 -- `Apply`, which
`0x656060` runs over every job from two other call sites and never from the tick.

**Two expiry styles, and the second one is loose by design.** `CTJ_PenaltyKeeper::Tick`
(`0x652080`) switches on the job's own id. Id 0 counts a seconds field down in the record
(`round(remaining - elapsed)`, the field read unsigned through the `+ 2^32` fixup at `0xb45ba4`)
and, at zero, re-arms for `0x2a300` = **48 hours** if penalty points remain. Every other id holds
an absolute `__time32_t` that `Create` wrote as `now + span` -- and the tick only reads the clock
once its accumulator at `+0xc` reaches the `10.0f` at `0xb45b44`, subtracting the `10.0` *double*
at `0xb45c60` rather than resetting. **A timestamp job can therefore outlive its expiry by up to
ten seconds**, and the periodic-not-reset subtraction means that slack never accumulates.

**A recorded fact was wrong, and the page had already disproved it.** `timed_jobs.md` said the
fourteen `_ADDTIMEDJOB` column getters at `+0x64..+0x98` are "fourteen consecutive getters on the
job object". `CTimedJob::PersistToDB` reads `piVar2 = *(int **)(param_1 + 8)` and calls them on
**that**. The page's own slot count settles it without the read: `CTimedJob` is a fifteen-slot
base and cannot have a slot 38, while the three common-data carriers have 39 slots each. Two of
those getters are now grounded by use rather than by position -- slot 26 is the category and slot
27 the id the lookup matches on -- along with the expiry pair, slot 28 to read and slot 13 to
write.

A third reading fell out for free: `CTJ_CoolTimeKeeper`'s slot 15 returns `owner + 8000`, and
8000 is `0x1f40` -- the SkillCooldowns block round 256 located independently from the other end.

`timedjob.PollAccumulator` and `timedjob.Countdown` carry the two styles with their constants
(`TickSeconds`, `WallClockPollSeconds`, `PenaltyPointsRearmSeconds`) and tests; the slot
constants are named, with the placeholders kept as aliases. Five names, one amended. In the same
pass the `SYSTEMS.md` Academy row was corrected: it still said the master role and the three
windows were unread, and both were recovered on 2026-09-17 -- the row had simply never caught up.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-second round: guild points are the skill points a member earns

The RE tick for 2026-09-19 20:47 took the Guild row's open item and it was sitting in a function
already read for another reason. `GObjPC_GainExpAndLevel`, right after the 400:1 skill-experience
conversion grants whole skill points (slot 93), adds the same count to `pc[0x861]` (pc+0x2184)
when the character has a guild, and once that exceeds 9 hands it to
`CGuildManager::RequestAddGuildPoints` (`0x5c62e0`: a PC, a guild, guild level below 6 -> `0x78F7
{guild, member, points}` to the global server) and resets it. The echo comes back through the
inter-server dispatcher to `CGuild::AddPoints` (`0x5c4110`): the guild's total at `guild+0x3c` and
the member's own contribution at `member+0x40` both grow by the count, and `0x38F5` types 5 and 6
tell the online members. **Guild points = skill points earned, one for one, in batches of at least
ten per member.** `guild.PointAccumulator` carries the rule with a test; srrevamp's guild has no
level or points total yet, so the wiring is a build item. Three names.

## Two-hundred-and-seventy-first round: two short negatives, each with its reason

The RE tick for 2026-09-19 20:32, docs only.

**The party flag byte's writer is on another server.** The invitee's answer builds a 0x1114-byte
request (`trs_wait_response::FUN_005be4f0`: a kind byte, the two ids, the invite record's `+0x34`
word, and for a fresh party two 0x68-byte member records with name, level, HP ratio and position)
and dispatches it through the request's slot 3 -- the party is created in the global/agent

`skill+0x168` -- itemdata column 68, the word BEFORE the `(code, values)` runs -- through the table
at `0xc63c7c`: 0 the ordinary instant action (20,460 rows), 1 the bow family's projectile action

## Two-hundred-and-sixty-fifth round: `efr` is the target pattern -- seven collectors, a radius, a cap and a 35 % falloff

The RE tick for 2026-09-19 19:05 opened the Skills row's "buff write path, start with `efr`" and
found `efr` is not a buff at all: it is how a skill picks its TARGETS.

**The dispatcher.** Both cast-context builders call `Skill_CollectTargetsByEffect` (`0x58cb70`)
before `Combat_ResolveDamage`: it asserts `value[1] <= 7`, forces kind 5 when `value[5]` is 4 or 5,
and dispatches `DAT_00c63f60[value[1]]` -- seven collectors in `.data` that fill the skill-use
context's target vector: **1 area around the caster, 2 area around the target, 3 a line from the
caster, 4 a line from the target, 5 the party, 6 a chain (the nearest others within
`value[2] x (value[3] + 1)`), 7 the monster's own group.** `value[2]` is the radius or half-width
(`Skill_WithinLine`, `0x58af60`: `sin(angle) x distance < BC + width`), `value[3]` the maximum
number of targets, **`value[4]` the falloff percent** -- every collector carries a share byte from
100 down by `round(share x (100 - v4) / 100)` per target added, the very byte the applier's mode 6
scales by -- and `value[5]` flags (bit 0 include self/primary).

**The data agrees.** Kinds 1/2/3/4/6/7 occur 3,184 / 3,992 / 1,062 / 844 / 1,531 / 39 times; the
falloff is 35 % on 6,725 area rows; the caps mostly 3 and 8. The spear's `PIERCE_D` is a two-target
line of half-width 2 at 25 %; the bow's multi-shot a kind-6 chain of three at 35 %.

**A correction.** SYSTEMS said `ApplySkillParamsToChar` reads the skill's `efr` field `0x28c`; that
read is the CHARACTER's `+0xa30` (an `int*` indexed by 0x28c), the active-effect book. `efr` is
read at the cast, by the damage resolver (mode 6) and by the applier's mode switch.

Recorded: `skill_params.md` "efr's values are the target pattern", `skillparam.EfrKind*` with the
value offsets and `AreaTargetShare` (100, 65, 42, 27 at 35 %) with a test, eleven names. **Not
wired**: srrevamp hits one target per cast; the pattern needs several results per cast and is a
build item. No shipped value changed; no release.

## Two-hundred-and-sixty-third round: the reuse delay is a descriptor -- and potions do not have one

The RE tick for 2026-09-19 18:33 followed round 262's array mapping one step further, to the
note from 2026-09-18 that srrevamp "enforces NO item cooldown" and that the column feeding the
item's reuse span "is not identified".

**The rule.** `RefObjItem::ExtractData` reads every `(Param, Desc128)` element's descriptor; one
containing `cooltime` (case-insensitive) is parsed as **`COOLTIME:<group>`** -- the group in hex
after `0x` or in decimal -- into `ref+0x520`, with that element's Param stored at `ref+0x524` as
the **cooltime in milliseconds** (a bad descriptor logs `invalid parameter has been assigned for
item cooltime: %s, %s`). `Item_HandleUseItem` (`0x510980`) refuses a use with **`0x185b`
`UIIT_MSG_STRGERR_WAIT_FOR_REUSE_DELAY`** while `ItemCooldowns::IsReady` (`0x64c040`, the skill
gate's own cooldown block, item groups in their own map) says the GROUP's timer is running, and
after the success reply `ItemCooldowns::Arm` (`0x64c320`) starts it for that many ms -- a delay of
300 000 ms or more taking a persisted branch (`time32`), so long cooldowns survive a relog.

**The data.** 148 retail rows carry a descriptor: the random-cure pills (group `0xC8`, 20 000 ms),
event and premium items from 5 s to 23 h, a few at 1 ms. **No HP, MP or vigour potion carries
one** -- the server puts no reuse delay on potions; whatever pacing the retail client applies to
potion clicks is the client's. So the 2026-09-18 "gap" was, for potions, the engine's own rule.

**Shipped (v0.1.407):** `refdata.Item.CooltimeGroup/CooltimeMs` as export columns 64-65 (the
exporter finds the descriptor the parser's way; a strict suffix, older files read 0/0 = no delay),
the SQL columns and round trip, `session/itemcooldown.go` (a per-character, per-group timer) and
the gate in `UseItemHandler` -- refused inside the timer, armed after success, in memory (the
300 s persistence is disclosed as unbuilt). Live but idle: the handler still consumes only restore
items, and none of those has a cooltime. Tests: the exporter's descriptor scan on the cure pill's
row shape, the tracker's group semantics. Two names.

**Data refreshed on the public server** (2026-09-19 18:47): items re-exported from the archive on
the box (66 columns, 15,338 rows, the transient extracts deleted) and imported -- `items` now
carries 101 rows with a cooltime (10374: group 200, 20 000 ms) and the elixirs' packed rates
(3675: 420744970 / 168430090 / 168101125). One export fix on the way: the Param columns of rows
that are not elixirs hold "-1" among other things, which the unsigned reader refused and aborted
the whole import; the exporter now writes 0 for anything that is not a dword and the reader
tolerates it. The public server picks the new server up from `dev`; the tag `v0.1.407` builds the
